LACHMAN.clue: Knee test at 20–30 degrees of flexion that checks anterior tibial translation and is preferred when swelling is acute
LACHMAN.rationale: A soft end-feel on this maneuver supports an anterior cruciate tear. It is preferred over a 90-degree drawer early after injury because hamstring guarding is less.

MCMURRAY.clue: Meniscal test that rotates the tibia while the knee is extended from full flexion; a click or joint-line pain is positive
MCMURRAY.rationale: External rotation of the tibia with valgus stresses the medial meniscus; internal rotation with varus stresses the lateral meniscus. Sensitivity is limited, so a negative test does not clear the knee.

APLEY.clue: Prone knee test: compression with rotation stresses the meniscus, while distraction with rotation stresses ligaments
APLEY.rationale: Pain with compression supports a meniscal lesion. Pain that appears instead when the tibia is distracted supports a ligament injury.

THESSALY.clue: Standing meniscal test in which the patient rotates the body on a slightly bent knee
THESSALY.rationale: The test is done first at about 5 degrees of flexion and then near 20. Joint-line pain, locking, or catching is a positive finding.

VALGUS.clue: Stress at 30 degrees of knee flexion that isolates the medial collateral ligament
VALGUS.rationale: Laxity only at 30 degrees points to the medial collateral ligament. Laxity also present at full extension implies additional capsule or cruciate injury.

VARUS.clue: Stress at 30 degrees of knee flexion that isolates the lateral collateral ligament
VARUS.rationale: The lateral collateral ligament does not attach to the lateral meniscus. Opening at full extension suggests a more extensive posterolateral or cruciate injury.

PIVOT.clue: Shift test that subluxes and then reduces the lateral tibial plateau in an anterior-cruciate-deficient knee
PIVOT.rationale: Valgus and internal rotation are applied as the knee is flexed from extension. A clunk near 20–40 degrees is positive and usually requires a relaxed patient.

GODFREY.clue: 90/90 sag of the tibia that indicates posterior cruciate insufficiency
GODFREY.rationale: With the hip and knee flexed to 90 degrees, the tibia drops backward relative to the femur. A posterior drawer at 90 degrees is the companion test.

DRAWER.clue: 90-degree knee test of straight anterior or posterior tibial translation
DRAWER.rationale: An anterior force tests the anterior cruciate but can be blocked by hamstring spasm or effusion. A posterior force tests the posterior cruciate.

DIAL.clue: Test comparing tibial external rotation at 30 and 90 degrees of knee flexion
DIAL.rationale: Extra rotation only at 30 degrees implicates the posterolateral corner. Extra rotation at both 30 and 90 degrees also implicates the posterior cruciate ligament.

SLOCUM.clue: Anterior drawer performed with the tibia rotated to detect rotary knee instability
SLOCUM.rationale: Internal rotation of the tibia biases the test toward anterolateral instability. External rotation biases it toward anteromedial instability.

NOBLE.clue: Compression of the iliotibial band over the lateral femoral condyle as the knee extends
NOBLE.rationale: Pain over the lateral femoral condyle near 30 degrees of flexion supports iliotibial band friction. The band is tightest as it crosses the condyle in that range.

OBER.clue: Sidelying test of iliotibial-band length: the hip is extended, then allowed to drop into adduction
OBER.rationale: If the thigh stays abducted, the iliotibial band or tensor fasciae latae is tight. The hip must not be allowed to flex or the test is invalid.

THOMAS.clue: Supine test in which one knee is pulled to the chest and the opposite thigh is watched
THOMAS.rationale: The opposite thigh lifting off the table indicates hip-flexor tightness. The knee extending on that side indicates rectus femoris tightness.

KENDALL.clue: Hip-flexor length test with the thigh hanging off the table edge so rectus femoris can be judged separately
KENDALL.rationale: If the thigh rises, the iliopsoas is tight. If the knee cannot stay flexed near 80 degrees, the rectus femoris is tight.

FABER.clue: Figure-4 test of flexion, abduction, and external rotation used to separate hip from sacroiliac pain
FABER.rationale: Posterior pain over the sacroiliac region suggests a sacroiliac source. Groin pain suggests the hip joint itself.

FADIR.clue: Hip test of flexion, adduction, and internal rotation used for labral irritation or femoroacetabular impingement
FADIR.rationale: Anterior groin pain is the positive finding. The test is sensitive but not specific, so imaging and the rest of the exam still matter.

SCOUR.clue: Hip test that compresses the femur into the acetabulum while sweeping an arc of flexion
SCOUR.rationale: Groin pain, clicking, or apprehension suggests an intra-articular source such as a labral tear or osteoarthritis. It is not a test of muscle length.

TRENDELENBURG.clue: Single-leg stance sign in which the pelvis drops on the side opposite a weak hip abductor
TRENDELENBURG.rationale: The drop is caused by weakness of the gluteus medius on the stance leg, or by the superior gluteal nerve. A trunk lean toward the stance leg is the compensated form.

THOMPSON.clue: Calf-squeeze test for a complete Achilles rupture; the foot should plantarflex if the tendon is intact
THOMPSON.rationale: The patient is prone with the foot off the table, and absent plantarflexion is positive. Weak plantarflexion can remain from other muscles, so a little motion does not prove the tendon is intact.

TALAR.clue: Tilt test: inversion stresses the calcaneofibular ligament and eversion stresses the deltoid ligament
TALAR.rationale: The anterior talofibular ligament is tested better by an anterior drawer of the ankle in slight plantarflexion. Inversion in more dorsiflexion biases the tilt toward the calcaneofibular ligament.

KLEIGER.clue: External-rotation stress of the foot that provokes a syndesmosis or deltoid injury
KLEIGER.rationale: Pain at the distal tibiofibular joint, especially in dorsiflexion, supports a high ankle sprain. Medial pain supports the deltoid ligament.

WINDLASS.clue: Test in which great-toe extension tightens the plantar fascia and raises the medial arch
WINDLASS.rationale: Pain at the medial calcaneal origin supports plantar fasciitis. The same mechanism stiffens the foot for push-off during gait.

MULDER.clue: Squeeze of the metatarsal heads that reproduces a click or web-space pain from an interdigital neuroma
MULDER.rationale: The third web space is the usual site. Narrow shoes aggravate it, and the pain is neuritic rather than a first-step heel pain.

HOMAN.clue: Calf pain on passive ankle dorsiflexion, once used for clotting but too inaccurate to rule a clot in or out
HOMAN.rationale: A negative finding does not exclude deep-vein thrombosis, and a positive finding is nonspecific. Diagnosis depends on history, swelling, and duplex imaging, not this maneuver.

HAWKINS.clue: Impingement test: the shoulder is flexed to 90 degrees and then forcibly internally rotated
HAWKINS.rationale: Pain implicates the subacromial tissues, including the supraspinatus tendon and bursa. It does not by itself prove a full-thickness cuff tear.

NEER.clue: Impingement test: the arm is passively elevated in internal rotation through the scapular plane
NEER.rationale: Pain at the end of elevation suggests subacromial compression. Scapular stabilization during the test keeps the motion at the glenohumeral joint.

PAINFUL.clue: Arc of abduction in which pain from about 60 to 120 degrees suggests a subacromial problem
PAINFUL.rationale: Pain only at the very top of elevation, near 170 degrees, points instead to the acromioclavicular joint. A mid-range arc is the subacromial pattern.

DROP.clue: Arm test: the patient cannot slowly lower the arm from abduction, suggesting a rotator-cuff tear
DROP.rationale: A sudden drop or severe pain is a positive finding and is associated with supraspinatus failure. Weakness should be compared with pain inhibition.

LIFTOFF.clue: Gerber test: the hand is lifted off the low back to isolate subscapularis
LIFTOFF.rationale: Inability to lift the hand, or the elbow falling back, is positive. If the patient cannot reach behind the back, a belly-press test is used instead.

BELLY.clue: Press test for subscapularis: the palm pushes into the abdomen and the elbow should stay forward
BELLY.rationale: The elbow dropping backward, or the wrist flexing to create pressure, means subscapularis is not holding internal rotation. It is useful when a lift-off position is impossible.

BEARHUG.clue: Subscapularis test: the hand rests on the opposite shoulder and the examiner tries to lift it away
BEARHUG.rationale: Failure to keep the hand on the shoulder indicates subscapularis weakness. It biases the upper portion of the muscle more than a lift-off does.

PATTE.clue: Resisted external rotation with the arm abducted in the scapular plane, aimed at infraspinatus
PATTE.rationale: Weakness or pain implicates infraspinatus and, to a lesser extent, teres minor. External rotation with the arm at the side is the companion screen.

HORNBLOWER.clue: Sign of teres minor weakness: the patient cannot externally rotate the shoulder in 90 degrees of abduction
HORNBLOWER.rationale: The arm falls into internal rotation instead of holding external rotation. Teres minor is innervated by the axillary nerve, unlike infraspinatus.

SPEED.clue: Resisted shoulder flexion with the elbow straight and the forearm supinated, for the long head of biceps
SPEED.rationale: Pain in the bicipital groove suggests biceps tendinopathy and can also occur with a superior labral tear. The test loads the tendon in its groove.

YERGASON.clue: Resisted supination with the elbow flexed, used for the biceps tendon and its restraining ligament
YERGASON.rationale: Pain in the bicipital groove is positive. A pop of the tendon out of the groove implicates the transverse humeral ligament.

OBRIEN.clue: Active compression test: downward force on the internally rotated, slightly adducted arm is repeated with the palm up
OBRIEN.rationale: Deep pain or clicking that improves with the palm up suggests a superior labral tear. Pain on top of the shoulder that does not change suggests the acromioclavicular joint.

CRANK.clue: Labral test: an axial load is applied to the humerus in abduction while the arm is rotated
CRANK.rationale: A click, clunk, or pain inside the shoulder suggests a labral tear. It is one of several labral tests and is not specific alone.

JERK.clue: Posterior labral test: axial load is applied as the flexed arm is moved across the body
JERK.rationale: A sudden clunk suggests a posteroinferior labral lesion. Pain without a clunk is less specific but can reflect posterior shoulder pain.

SULCUS.clue: A groove appearing under the acromion when the arm is pulled downward, indicating inferior instability
SULCUS.rationale: A visible or measurable gap supports multidirectional or inferior glenohumeral laxity. Compare with the other side and ask whether symptoms are reproduced.

RELOCATION.clue: Test in which a posterior force on the humeral head relieves fear in the abducted, externally rotated position
RELOCATION.rationale: Relief of apprehension supports anterior glenohumeral instability. Increased pain instead of relief suggests that the test is irritating the cuff or labrum rather than reducing a subluxation.

CROSS.clue: Body-adduction test that compresses the acromioclavicular joint
CROSS.rationale: Pain localized on top of the shoulder is positive for the acromioclavicular joint. Deep pain is less specific and can come from the cuff or labrum.

ROOS.clue: Elevated-arm stress test: the patient opens and closes the fists for three minutes with shoulders and elbows at 90 degrees
ROOS.rationale: Heaviness, numbness, or color change supports thoracic-outlet compression. It is a symptom test, not proof of a single anatomical site.

ADSON.clue: Thoracic-outlet test: the head rotates toward the tested arm, the neck extends, and the patient inhales
ADSON.rationale: A diminished radial pulse or reproduced symptoms implicates the scalene triangle. Pulse change alone is common in asymptomatic people, so symptom reproduction matters.

WRIGHT.clue: Hyperabduction test for thoracic outlet compression under pectoralis minor
WRIGHT.rationale: The arm is raised overhead and the radial pulse and symptoms are monitored. A change suggests the subcoracoid space, not necessarily the scalenes.

MILITARY.clue: Brace posture that narrows the costoclavicular space to screen thoracic-outlet compression
MILITARY.rationale: The shoulders are drawn down and back. Loss of the radial pulse or symptom reproduction is a positive finding for that space.

ALLEN.clue: Circulatory test of the wrist: both arteries are occluded, then one is released and color should return promptly
ALLEN.rationale: Delayed refill means that artery is not adequately patent. It is used before procedures that rely on the radial artery, and it is not the hyperabduction outlet test.

PHALEN.clue: Wrist-flexion test held up to a minute to reproduce median-nerve symptoms
PHALEN.rationale: Paresthesia in the thumb, index, middle, or radial half of the ring finger supports carpal tunnel syndrome. Wrist extension, the prayer position, is the reverse form.

REVERSE.clue: Prayer-position wrist test: sustained extension reproduces median-nerve symptoms at the carpal tunnel
REVERSE.rationale: It is the opposite of the wrist-flexion version. Symptom location should match the median digits, not the ulnar fingers.

TINEL.clue: Percussion over a nerve that reproduces distal tingling in the nerve's distribution
TINEL.rationale: At the wrist it screens the median nerve; at the elbow, the ulnar nerve; behind the medial malleolus, the tibial nerve. It is specific only when the tingling is in the correct distribution.

DURKAN.clue: Direct pressure over the carpal tunnel that reproduces median paresthesia
DURKAN.rationale: Compression is held for about 30 seconds. It is often more sensitive than wrist flexion alone for carpal tunnel syndrome.

FROMENT.clue: Paper-pinch sign: the thumb interphalangeal joint flexes to substitute for a weak adductor pollicis
FROMENT.rationale: Adductor pollicis is ulnar-innervated. Flexor pollicis longus, which substitutes, is median-innervated via the anterior interosseous nerve.

WARTENBERG.clue: Ulnar-nerve sign: the little finger rests abducted and cannot adduct
WARTENBERG.rationale: The palmar interosseous muscle to the little finger is ulnar-innervated. This resting posture is different from a sensory test of the superficial radial nerve that shares the same eponym.

COZEN.clue: Resisted wrist extension with the forearm pronated, provoking lateral elbow pain
COZEN.rationale: Pain at the lateral epicondyle supports extensor-tendon overload, especially extensor carpi radialis brevis. Passive stretch into wrist flexion and pronation is the companion test.

MILL.clue: Passive stretch into forearm pronation and wrist flexion with the elbow extended, for lateral elbow tendinopathy
MILL.rationale: Pain at the lateral epicondyle is positive. It lengthens the wrist extensors rather than asking them to contract.

MAUDSLEY.clue: Resisted middle-finger extension that provokes lateral elbow or radial-tunnel pain
MAUDSLEY.rationale: Extensor carpi radialis brevis is loaded by this test. It does not distinguish a tendon source from radial-tunnel irritation by itself.

GOLFER.clue: Elbow provocation: pain at the medial epicondyle with resisted wrist flexion
GOLFER.rationale: The wrist flexors and pronator teres share the medial epicondyle. Ulnar-nerve symptoms should be separated from a pure tendon pain.

FINKELSTEIN.clue: Thumb-in-fist ulnar deviation that provokes pain in the first dorsal compartment
FINKELSTEIN.rationale: A positive test supports de Quervain tenosynovitis of abductor pollicis longus and extensor pollicis brevis. Pain should be at the radial styloid, not the ulnar wrist.

SPURLING.clue: Cervical compression in extension and sidebending toward the painful side that reproduces arm pain
SPURLING.rationale: Reproduction of radicular pain supports foraminal nerve-root compression; local neck pain alone is not a positive finding. Specificity is better than sensitivity.

DISTRACTION.clue: Cervical test: an upward lift that eases arm pain supports nerve-root compression
DISTRACTION.rationale: Relief of radicular symptoms is the positive finding. Increased pain can occur with muscle or ligament injury and does not support a compressive root lesion.

SLUMP.clue: Seated neural-tension test combining spinal flexion, knee extension, and ankle dorsiflexion
SLUMP.rationale: A positive test reproduces the patient's neural symptoms, and those symptoms ease when neck flexion is released. That structural differentiation separates nerve tension from hamstring tightness.

STRAIGHT.clue: Leg-raise test: passive hip flexion with the knee extended reproduces radicular pain, classically between 30 and 70 degrees
STRAIGHT.rationale: Pain only at the end of the raise is often hamstring tightness, and adding ankle dorsiflexion increases neural tension. Raising the opposite leg is more specific for a disc herniation when it reproduces the involved-side pain.

BRAGARD.clue: Addition of ankle dorsiflexion to a straight-leg raise to increase sciatic neural tension
BRAGARD.rationale: If lowering the leg slightly relieves pain and dorsiflexion brings it back, the test supports a neural rather than only a muscular limit.

CROSSED.clue: Straight-leg raise of the uninvolved limb that reproduces pain in the involved limb
CROSSED.rationale: This finding is highly specific for a large lumbar disc herniation. It is less sensitive, so its absence does not rule a herniation out.

KEMP.clue: Lumbar quadrant test combining extension with sidebending and rotation
KEMP.rationale: Local low-back pain is often interpreted as facet loading, while pain radiating into the leg suggests foraminal compression. The test is provocative, not definitive.

PURSER.clue: Test for atlantoaxial instability in which a posterior force through the forehead reduces excessive anterior translation
PURSER.rationale: A clunk or a reduction of symptoms is positive and implies transverse-ligament laxity. A positive result is a reason to avoid end-range cervical techniques and to refer.

ALAR.clue: Ligament test: the spinous process of C2 should move immediately as the head is sidebent or rotated
ALAR.rationale: A lag before C2 moves suggests alar-ligament insufficiency. Do not apply end-range force if instability is suspected.

VERTEBRAL.clue: Artery screen using sustained end-range cervical rotation and extension, which does not reliably clear vascular risk
VERTEBRAL.rationale: Dizziness, diplopia, dysarthria, dysphagia, drop attacks, nausea, nystagmus, or facial numbness are warning symptoms. A negative screen does not rule out arterial disease, and a concerning history stops manual treatment.

LASLETT.clue: Cluster of sacroiliac provocation tests used together because no single test is accurate enough
LASLETT.rationale: Distraction, compression, thigh thrust, sacral thrust, and Gaenslen's test are the usual group. Several positive tests, in a patient whose pain is not explained by the disc, support a sacroiliac source.

GAENSLEN.clue: Sacroiliac test: one hip is flexed to the chest while the other thigh hangs into extension
GAENSLEN.rationale: Pain in the sacroiliac region on the extended side is the usual positive finding. Hip-joint pain can also be provoked, so the location of pain matters.

THIGH.clue: Thrust test: a posterior force through the flexed femur provokes sacroiliac pain
THIGH.rationale: The hip is flexed to about 90 degrees and the force is directed through the femur. Reproduction of the patient's buttock pain is positive.

ROMBERG.clue: Feet-together stance that gets much worse when the eyes close, pointing to sensory rather than cerebellar ataxia
ROMBERG.rationale: Cerebellar ataxia is present even with the eyes open. A marked increase in sway only after the eyes close implicates dorsal-column or peripheral sensory loss.

PRONATOR.clue: Drift test: with the arms forward and eyes closed, one forearm turns and the arm sinks
PRONATOR.rationale: This subtle sign supports a mild corticospinal lesion on the opposite side. It is not the forearm muscle that shares the name.

BABINSKI.clue: Plantar response in which the great toe extends after the lateral sole is stroked, indicating an upper motor neuron lesion
BABINSKI.rationale: An extensor response is normal in infancy and becomes pathologic once the child is walking, commonly cited after 12 to 24 months. Fanning of the toes may accompany it.

HOFFMAN.clue: Flick of the middle-finger nail that produces thumb flexion, a cervical upper-motor-neuron sign
HOFFMAN.rationale: A positive sign suggests corticospinal-tract irritation, often in the cervical cord. It is interpreted with imaging and other long-tract signs, not alone.

CLONUS.clue: Rhythmic, repeated beats of a muscle after a quick sustained stretch, classically at the ankle
CLONUS.rationale: Sustained beats indicate an upper motor neuron lesion. A beat or two that stops can be normal, especially if symmetric and unsustained.

KERNIG.clue: Meningeal test: with the hip flexed, knee extension causes pain or resistance in the spine
KERNIG.rationale: It is used with neck stiffness and systemic signs to support meningeal irritation. A positive finding needs urgent medical evaluation, not stretching.

BRUDZINSKI.clue: Meningeal sign: passive neck flexion causes the hips and knees to flex
BRUDZINSKI.rationale: It indicates meningeal irritation and is an emergency finding when paired with fever or headache. It is not a neural-tension test for a lumbar disc.

LHERMITTE.clue: Electric sensation down the spine on neck flexion, classically from dorsal-column irritation
LHERMITTE.rationale: It is associated with multiple sclerosis, cervical stenosis, and vitamin B12 deficiency. The symptom is a warning to evaluate the cord, not a cue to mobilize into flexion.

ASHWORTH.clue: Ordinal scale of resistance to passive stretch, with a 1+ grade added in the modified version
ASHWORTH.rationale: Scores run from 0 (no increase) to 4 (rigid). The scale does not standardize stretch speed, so it mixes spasticity with soft-tissue stiffness.

TARDIEU.clue: Scale that compares the angle of muscle reaction at slow versus fast speed
TARDIEU.rationale: The difference between the slow full range and the fast catch is the spasticity angle. It separates velocity-dependent reflex tone from a fixed contracture.

JENDRASSIK.clue: Reinforcement maneuver in which the patient pulls the hooked fingers apart while a reflex is tested
JENDRASSIK.rationale: Distraction and remote muscle contraction can bring out a reflex that is hard to elicit. It does not change a truly absent reflex into a normal one.

HALLPIKE.clue: Positional maneuver: the patient is moved quickly from sitting to supine with the head extended and rotated about 45 degrees
HALLPIKE.rationale: A latent, brief, upbeating torsional nystagmus that fatigues supports posterior-canal benign positional vertigo of the downward ear. Immediate or purely vertical nystagmus that does not fatigue suggests a central cause.

EPLEY.clue: Canalith repositioning sequence that moves posterior-canal debris back toward the utricle
EPLEY.rationale: Treatment starts in the provoking position, then the head is turned and the patient rolls until sitting. It treats the canalithiasis form of posterior-canal positional vertigo.

CANAL.clue: Supine roll test turns the head each way to screen the horizontal semicircular duct for positional vertigo
CANAL.rationale: Direction-changing horizontal nystagmus is the finding. The side with the stronger response helps identify which ear is involved.

HINTS.clue: Bedside battery of head impulse, nystagmus, and skew used in acute continuous vertigo
HINTS.rationale: A normal head impulse, direction-changing nystagmus, or a skew deviation suggests a central cause. An abnormal impulse with unidirectional nystagmus and no skew fits a peripheral lesion.

IMPULSE.clue: Head test: a quick turn toward a weak labyrinth makes the eyes slip off target, then correct with a saccade
IMPULSE.rationale: A corrective saccade means the vestibulo-ocular reflex is weak on that side. During acute continuous vertigo, a normal result raises concern for stroke rather than a peripheral lesion.

FUKUDA.clue: Stepping test done with the eyes closed; excessive rotation suggests vestibular asymmetry
FUKUDA.rationale: The patient marches in place for many steps. Marked turning is a screening sign and does not replace positional testing or a full oculomotor exam.

COVER.clue: Test of ocular alignment: covering one eye and then the other reveals a refixation if the eyes are skewed
COVER.rationale: A vertical refixation is the skew component of the acute vestibular battery. Its presence in acute vertigo is treated as a central sign.

ORTOLANI.clue: Infant hip maneuver that reduces a dislocated hip with abduction and a gentle lift
ORTOLANI.rationale: A clunk of reduction is positive for developmental dysplasia. A click without a clunk is not the same finding.

BARLOW.clue: Infant hip maneuver that tries to dislocate an unstable hip with adduction and posterior pressure
BARLOW.rationale: A clunk of exit is positive. The hip that can be displaced is then checked to see whether it reduces.

OTTAWA.clue: Decision rules for when ankle, foot, or knee radiographs are needed after injury
OTTAWA.rationale: Ankle films are indicated with malleolar bone tenderness or inability to take four steps. Knee films are indicated by age 55 or older, fibular-head or isolated patellar tenderness, inability to flex to 90 degrees, or inability to bear weight four steps.

CRAIG.clue: Prone test that estimates femoral anteversion from the leg angle when the greater trochanter is most prominent
CRAIG.rationale: Adult values are normally about 8 to 15 degrees. Markedly higher anteversion is associated with in-toeing and more internal than external rotation.

SCHOBER.clue: Skin-mark test of lumbar flexion; little separation of the marks means motion is limited
SCHOBER.rationale: A modified version marks 10 cm above and 5 cm below the lumbosacral junction. An increase of less than about 5 cm is restricted and is used in ankylosing spondylitis.

ADAMS.clue: Forward-bend screen for scoliosis in which a rib hump appears on the convex side
ADAMS.rationale: The hump is produced by vertebral rotation, not by a leg-length difference alone. A positive screen is followed by measurement of the curve.

COBB.clue: Angle of a spinal curve measured between the most tilted vertebrae at each end
COBB.rationale: The angle guides whether a growing child is observed, braced, or referred. Curves are still named by the side of the convexity.

RISSER.clue: Sign of iliac-crest ossification used to estimate how much spinal growth remains
RISSER.rationale: Lower grades mean the skeleton is immature and a scoliotic curve can still progress. It is used with the curve magnitude when considering a brace.

SUPRASPINATUS.clue: Rotator-cuff muscle tested by the empty-can position: elevation in the scapular plane with the thumb down
SUPRASPINATUS.rationale: It is innervated by the suprascapular nerve (C5–C6), initiates abduction, and is compressed in the subacromial space. Pain or weakness in the empty-can test implicates this muscle or its tendon.

INFRASPINATUS.clue: Rotator-cuff muscle that externally rotates the shoulder and is tested with the arm at the side
INFRASPINATUS.rationale: The suprascapular nerve innervates it. Weak external rotation with the elbow at the side points here more than to teres minor, which is tested in abduction.

DELTOID.clue: Muscle that abducts the humerus and is innervated by the axillary nerve
DELTOID.rationale: The middle fibers abduct, the anterior fibers flex and internally rotate, and the posterior fibers extend and externally rotate. Loss of this muscle flattens the shoulder contour.

AXILLARY.clue: Nerve from C5–C6 that innervates deltoid and teres minor and supplies skin over the lateral shoulder
AXILLARY.rationale: It is at risk with a surgical-neck fracture and with anterior shoulder dislocation. The patient cannot abduct the arm and has a sensory patch on the outer shoulder.

SERRATUS.clue: Anterior muscle that protracts and upwardly rotates the scapula; its palsy causes medial winging
SERRATUS.rationale: The long thoracic nerve (C5–C7) innervates it. Winging increases with shoulder flexion or a wall push, and overhead elevation is limited.

WINGING.clue: Scapular sign of serratus anterior or trapezius weakness, seen as the medial border lifting off the rib cage
WINGING.rationale: Long-thoracic palsy makes winging worse with forward flexion. Spinal-accessory palsy weakens the shrug and disturbs upward rotation during abduction.

TRAPEZIUS.clue: Scapular muscle innervated by the spinal accessory nerve that elevates, retracts, and upwardly rotates the scapula
TRAPEZIUS.rationale: Upper fibers shrug, middle fibers retract, and lower fibers depress and upwardly rotate with serratus anterior. A cranial-nerve XI lesion weakens the shrug and head turn.

ACCESSORY.clue: Cranial nerve XI, which innervates trapezius and sternocleidomastoid
ACCESSORY.rationale: The sternocleidomastoid rotates the head to the opposite side and sidebends to the same side. Testing includes a shrug and resisted head turn.

LATISSIMUS.clue: Muscle innervated by the thoracodorsal nerve that extends, adducts, and internally rotates the shoulder
LATISSIMUS.rationale: The nerve arises from C6–C8. Patients with lower cervical cord injury who still have this muscle can use it to depress the shoulder and lift the pelvis for transfers.

RHOMBOID.clue: Scapular retractor and downward rotator innervated by the dorsal scapular nerve
RHOMBOID.rationale: The dorsal scapular nerve is C4–C5. Weakness contributes to poor scapular stability and a different winging pattern than serratus anterior palsy.

LEVATOR.clue: Scapulae muscle that elevates the scapula and assists downward rotation, innervated by the dorsal scapular nerve
LEVATOR.rationale: It attaches the transverse processes of the upper cervical spine to the superior angle of the scapula. It is an accessory breathing muscle only indirectly; its main role is scapular elevation.

PECTORALIS.clue: Major muscle that adducts and internally rotates the humerus and is innervated by both pectoral nerves
PECTORALIS.rationale: The lateral pectoral nerve supplies the clavicular head and the medial pectoral nerve also reaches the sternocostal head. The smaller muscle deep to it, pectoralis minor, is medial-pectoral only and can compress the neurovascular bundle.

MINOR.clue: Pectoralis muscle that anteriorly tilts the scapula and can compress vessels and nerves near the coracoid
MINOR.rationale: The medial pectoral nerve innervates it. Tightness is one site of thoracic-outlet compression, tested with hyperabduction.

MAJOR.clue: Teres muscle that extends, adducts, and internally rotates the shoulder and shares the little-helper role of latissimus
MAJOR.rationale: The lower subscapular nerve innervates it, not the axillary nerve. Teres minor is the axillary-innervated external rotator and should not be confused with this muscle.

CORACOID.clue: Scapular process that anchors pectoralis minor, coracobrachialis, and the short head of biceps
CORACOID.rationale: The neurovascular bundle passes deep to pectoralis minor near this process. Tenderness and a prominent process are landmarks for that outlet space.

ACROMION.clue: Scapular process that forms the roof of the subacromial space
ACROMION.rationale: A hooked shape narrows the outlet for the supraspinatus tendon and bursa. Impingement tests drive the greater tuberosity toward this roof.

CLAVICLE.clue: Bone whose middle third is the most common fracture site and whose displacement can threaten the brachial plexus
CLAVICLE.rationale: The subclavian vessels and lower plexus lie behind the medial shaft. Most fractures heal in a sling; marked displacement or neurovascular change needs urgent referral.

SCAPULA.clue: Triangular bone that must upwardly rotate for full overhead elevation
SCAPULA.rationale: Full elevation is about two parts glenohumeral motion and one part scapular motion, roughly 120 and 60 degrees. Loss of upward rotation limits flexion and abduction.

RHYTHM.clue: Scapulohumeral pattern in which full arm elevation is about two parts glenohumeral motion to one part scapular motion
RHYTHM.rationale: About 120 degrees comes from the glenohumeral joint and 60 from the scapula. The first 30 degrees are mostly glenohumeral, the so-called setting phase.

HUMERUS.clue: Arm bone whose surgical neck is associated with axillary-nerve injury and whose shaft is associated with radial-nerve injury
HUMERUS.rationale: Anterior shoulder dislocation also risks the axillary nerve. A midshaft fracture can produce wrist drop from the radial nerve in the spiral groove.

BICEPS.clue: Two-headed muscle innervated by the musculocutaneous nerve that flexes the elbow and supinates the forearm
BICEPS.rationale: The long head also flexes the shoulder and stabilizes the humeral head. Reflex testing of this muscle screens C5–C6.

POPEYE.clue: Deformity in which the biceps belly balls up after the long-head tendon ruptures
POPEYE.rationale: It is common in older adults and often causes less functional loss than the appearance suggests because the short head remains. Distal rupture at the radial tuberosity is a different, more disabling injury.

BRACHIALIS.clue: Primary elbow flexor that works in every forearm position and is innervated mainly by the musculocutaneous nerve
BRACHIALIS.rationale: Unlike biceps, it does not supinate. The radial nerve supplies a lateral portion, but the musculocutaneous nerve is the main innervation.

TRICEPS.clue: Elbow extensor innervated by the radial nerve, whose reflex screens C7
TRICEPS.rationale: The long head also adducts the shoulder. Loss of elbow extension after a cord injury removes the ability to perform a seated push-up for transfers.

OLECRANON.clue: Proximal ulnar process where the triceps inserts and a common site of bursitis
OLECRANON.rationale: A fracture here can interrupt elbow extension. Swelling over the tip is bursitis until infection is excluded, especially if the skin is broken.

RADIUS.clue: Forearm bone whose head is palpated just distal to the lateral epicondyle and whose distal end is the usual site of a dinner-fork fracture
RADIUS.rationale: The radial head is compressed during pronation and supination. A distal fracture with dorsal displacement is the Colles pattern.

ULNA.clue: Forearm bone that forms the hinge of the elbow and whose proximal fracture can dislocate the radial head
ULNA.rationale: That combination is a Monteggia injury, and the radial nerve may be involved. The styloid is on the ulnar side of the wrist.

MONTEGGIA.clue: Fracture of the ulna with dislocation of the radial head
MONTEGGIA.rationale: The radial or posterior interosseous nerve can be injured. Any ulnar fracture should be checked for a radial-head dislocation so it is not missed.

COLLES.clue: Distal radius fracture with dorsal displacement, the dinner-fork deformity from a fall on an outstretched hand
COLLES.rationale: Median-nerve compression can accompany it. The reverse pattern, with volar displacement, is a Smith fracture.

SMITH.clue: Distal radius fracture with volar displacement, the reverse of the dorsal dinner-fork pattern
SMITH.rationale: It typically follows a fall on a flexed wrist. Management still has to protect the median nerve and restore alignment.

NURSEMAID.clue: Radial-head subluxation in a young child after a longitudinal pull on a pronated forearm
NURSEMAID.rationale: The child will not use the arm and holds it slightly flexed. Supination with elbow flexion usually reduces it.

CARRYING.clue: Slight valgus angle of the extended elbow, normally larger in women
CARRYING.rationale: Excessive valgus can stretch the ulnar nerve at the cubital tunnel. A varus deformity after a childhood supracondylar fracture is called a gunstock deformity.

GUNSTOCK.clue: Varus deformity of the elbow that can follow a supracondylar humerus fracture in a child
GUNSTOCK.rationale: The normal elbow has a slight valgus angle, so varus is abnormal. The original fracture also risks the brachial artery and the median nerve.

CUBITAL.clue: Tunnel behind the medial epicondyle where the ulnar nerve is compressed, especially in flexion
CUBITAL.rationale: Symptoms are numbness in the ring and little fingers and intrinsic weakness. Night splinting in slight extension reduces traction on the nerve.

GUYON.clue: Canal at the wrist where the ulnar nerve can be compressed between the pisiform and the hook of the hamate
GUYON.rationale: Dorsal hand sensation is spared because that cutaneous branch leaves proximal to the canal. Cyclists and hook-of-hamate fractures are classic causes.

RADIAL.clue: Nerve that extends the wrist, fingers, and elbow and whose compression in the spiral groove causes wrist drop
RADIAL.rationale: A high lesion weakens triceps. A posterior interosseous lesion spares sensation and spares extensor carpi radialis longus, so the wrist extends with radial deviation.

PIN.clue: Motor branch of the radial nerve: finger extension is lost, sensation is spared, and wrist extension drifts radially
PIN.rationale: Extensor carpi radialis longus is spared because it is innervated before this branch. Compression often occurs at the arcade of Frohse in the supinator.

FROHSE.clue: Arcade in the supinator where the posterior interosseous nerve can be compressed
FROHSE.rationale: The result is finger and thumb extension weakness without sensory loss. Pain is in the proximal lateral forearm and is provoked by resisted supination.

MEDIAN.clue: Nerve compressed in the carpal tunnel; palmar sensation is spared because that branch enters outside the tunnel
MEDIAN.rationale: Symptoms wake the patient with tingling in the radial three and a half digits, and thenar muscles weaken late. A more proximal lesion also involves palm sensation.

AIN.clue: Pure motor branch of the median nerve: the patient cannot flex the thumb tip or the index fingertip
AIN.rationale: Pinch collapses pulp-to-pulp instead of tip-to-tip, and there is no sensory loss. Flexor pollicis longus and the lateral half of flexor digitorum profundus are the muscles.

CTS.clue: Median-nerve compression at the wrist with nocturnal paresthesia and, late, thenar wasting
CTS.rationale: The palmar cutaneous branch is spared. Phalen, Tinel, and carpal-compression tests are used, and thenar strength is compared with the other hand.

ULNAR.clue: Nerve of the intrinsic hand muscles, flexor carpi ulnaris, and the medial half of flexor digitorum profundus
ULNAR.rationale: Entrapment occurs at the cubital tunnel or in Guyon's canal. Clawing is often worse with a wrist lesion than an elbow lesion because the deep finger flexors still flex the fingertips.

LOAF.clue: Mnemonic for the median-innervated intrinsic hand muscles
LOAF.rationale: The muscles are the lateral two lumbricals, opponens pollicis, abductor pollicis brevis, and the superficial head of flexor pollicis brevis. The rest of the intrinsics are ulnar.

THENAR.clue: Thumb-side muscle mass innervated by the recurrent median nerve
THENAR.rationale: Wasting flattens the mound and limits opposition, the ape-hand posture. Sensation of the palm can still be intact in carpal tunnel syndrome.

HYPOTHENAR.clue: Little-finger muscle mass innervated by the ulnar nerve
HYPOTHENAR.rationale: It includes abductor, flexor, and opponens digiti minimi. Wasting accompanies an ulnar lesion at the wrist or elbow.

LUMBRICALS.clue: Muscles that flex the metacarpophalangeal joints and extend the interphalangeal joints
LUMBRICALS.rationale: The lateral two are median-innervated and the medial two are ulnar-innervated. Loss contributes to clawing.

INTEROSSEI.clue: Ulnar-innervated hand muscles; the palmar group adducts the fingers and the dorsal group abducts them
INTEROSSEI.rationale: A simple memory is palmar adduct and dorsal abduct. Wasting creates gutters between the metacarpals.

CLAW.clue: Resting posture of hyperextended knuckles and flexed finger joints from intrinsic-muscle loss
CLAW.rationale: An ulnar lesion produces it in the ring and little fingers. It is different from the median-nerve posture that appears only when the patient tries to make a fist.

BENEDICTION.clue: Posture seen when a median-nerve lesion prevents flexion of the index and middle fingers during a fist attempt
BENEDICTION.rationale: Flexor digitorum superficialis and the lateral half of profundus are weak, so those fingers stay extended. This is an active posture, not the resting ulnar claw.

SATURDAY.clue: Night palsy from radial-nerve compression against the humerus, producing wrist and finger drop
SATURDAY.rationale: Elbow extension is often spared if the lesion is distal to the triceps branches. Sensation is lost on the dorsal hand.

SCAPHOID.clue: Carpal bone with a retrograde blood supply, so a waist fracture can necrose the proximal pole
SCAPHOID.rationale: The anatomical snuffbox is tender. Because early films can miss the fracture, a suspected injury is immobilized and reimaged.

LUNATE.clue: Carpal bone whose avascular necrosis is Kienbock disease and whose dislocation follows a high-energy wrist injury
LUNATE.rationale: It sits in the proximal row and articulates with the radius. Unexplained dorsal wrist pain and stiffness after load should not be dismissed as a sprain.

KIENBOCK.clue: Avascular necrosis of the lunate, causing dorsal wrist pain and stiffness
KIENBOCK.rationale: It may follow trauma or repetitive load. Grip weakness and tenderness over the lunate warrant imaging rather than a tendon diagnosis alone.

HAMATE.clue: Carpal bone whose hook can fracture in golf or baseball and irritate the ulnar nerve
HAMATE.rationale: The hook forms the ulnar border of Guyon's canal. Ulnar-sided pain and intrinsic weakness after a stick-sport injury suggest this fracture.

PISIFORM.clue: Sesamoid carpal in the flexor carpi ulnaris tendon and the ulnar border of Guyon's canal
PISIFORM.rationale: It is a landmark for ulnar-nerve compression at the wrist. Tenderness is distinguished from a hook-of-hamate fracture.

TRAPEZIUM.clue: Carpal bone that forms the saddle joint with the first metacarpal
TRAPEZIUM.rationale: Osteoarthritis of this joint causes pain at the base of the thumb with pinch and grip. It is distal to the scaphoid in the snuffbox floor.

CAPITATE.clue: Largest carpal and the central axis of wrist motion
CAPITATE.rationale: It sits in the distal row and articulates with the lunate and the third metacarpal. Avascular risk is lower than for the scaphoid or lunate.

TRIQUETRUM.clue: Carpal on the ulnar side of the proximal row, between the lunate and the pisiform region
TRIQUETRUM.rationale: It can be tender after a fall and is part of the ulnar-sided differential with the triangular fibrocartilage. It is not the hook that borders Guyon's canal.

DEQUERVAIN.clue: Tenosynovitis of abductor pollicis longus and extensor pollicis brevis in the first dorsal compartment
DEQUERVAIN.rationale: Pain is at the radial styloid and the thumb-in-fist ulnar-deviation test is positive. New parents and repetitive thumb work are typical histories.

DUPUYTREN.clue: Contracture of the palmar fascia that flexes the ring and little fingers; sensation is normal and the tendon is not the diseased tissue
DUPUYTREN.rationale: The patient cannot lay the hand flat on a table. Stretching does not reverse a cord, and referral is based on how much the contracture limits function.

TRIGGER.clue: Finger that catches or locks because a flexor tendon cannot glide through the A1 pulley
TRIGGER.rationale: A nodule is often palpable at the pulley in the distal palm. The digit may lock in flexion and then snap straight.

PULLEY.clue: Fibrous loop that keeps a flexor tendon against the phalanx; the A2 and A4 loops are the most important to preserve
PULLEY.rationale: Loss of those two allows bowstringing and weakens flexion. The A1 loop is the usual site of a trigger digit and can be released.

MALLET.clue: Finger deformity: the distal joint rests in flexion because the extensor tendon has avulsed
MALLET.rationale: Treatment is continuous extension splinting of the distal joint while the proximal joint stays free to move. The splint is typically worn for six to eight weeks.

BOUTONNIERE.clue: Deformity of proximal-joint flexion and distal-joint hyperextension from a central-slip injury
BOUTONNIERE.rationale: The lateral bands slip volar to the proximal joint axis. The proximal joint is splinted in extension and the distal joint is left free to move.

SWAN.clue: Neck deformity: hyperextension of the proximal finger joint and flexion of the distal joint
SWAN.rationale: It occurs in rheumatoid arthritis and after an untreated mallet injury. It is the mechanical opposite of a boutonniere deformity.

JERSEY.clue: Finger injury in which flexor digitorum profundus avulses, usually from the ring finger
JERSEY.rationale: The patient cannot flex the distal joint when the proximal joint is stabilized. It often needs surgical repair rather than a splint alone.

SKIER.clue: Thumb injury: tear of the ulnar collateral ligament at the metacarpophalangeal joint
SKIER.rationale: Valgus laxity is tested with the joint slightly flexed. A complete tear can be blocked from healing by the adductor aponeurosis, the Stener lesion.

STENER.clue: Lesion in which the adductor aponeurosis blocks a fully torn thumb ulnar collateral ligament from healing closed
STENER.rationale: It is associated with a complete gamekeeper or skier tear. Marked laxity compared with the other thumb prompts surgical referral.

LAND.clue: Zone II of the finger flexors, where both tendons share a tight sheath and repairs have historically done poorly
LAND.rationale: The zone runs from the A1 pulley region to the superficialis insertion. Adhesions are common, so protected motion protocols are used after repair.

BENNETT.clue: Intra-articular fracture-dislocation of the base of the first metacarpal
BENNETT.rationale: The abductor pollicis longus pulls a fragment. It is less comminuted than a Rolando fracture of the same base and usually needs reduction.

ROLANDO.clue: Comminuted intra-articular fracture of the base of the first metacarpal
ROLANDO.rationale: It is a more fragmented injury than a Bennett fracture. Thumb opposition and pinch remain painful until the joint surface is restored.

JONES.clue: Fracture at the metaphyseal-diaphyseal junction of the fifth metatarsal, in a watershed with higher nonunion risk
JONES.rationale: It is proximal to a tuberosity avulsion from fibularis brevis, which heals more readily. A Jones fracture is often kept non-weight-bearing.

TFCC.clue: Triangular fibrocartilage of the ulnar wrist that stabilizes the distal radioulnar joint
TFCC.rationale: Injury causes ulnar-sided wrist pain with loading and rotation. It is distinguished from a hook-of-hamate fracture and from extensor carpi ulnaris tendinopathy.

FDS.clue: Muscle that flexes the proximal interphalangeal joints and is innervated by the median nerve
FDS.rationale: It is tested by holding the other fingers extended, which blocks the profundus, and asking for proximal-joint flexion. It travels with the profundus and the median nerve through the carpal tunnel.

FDP.clue: Muscle that flexes the distal finger joints; the lateral half is median (anterior interosseous) and the medial half is ulnar
FDP.rationale: The distal joint is tested with the proximal joint stabilized. Avulsion of its insertion is a jersey finger.

FCU.clue: Wrist flexor and ulnar deviator innervated by the ulnar nerve, inserting via the pisiform
FCU.rationale: It is weak in an ulnar lesion at the elbow but spared in a lesion only at Guyon's canal. The ulnar nerve enters the forearm through this muscle's two heads.

EHL.clue: Deep-fibular muscle that extends the great toe; its strength is the L5 myotome screen
EHL.rationale: Weakness with a preserved ankle jerk and sensory change on the dorsum of the foot fits an L5 root. The tendon is visible on the dorsum of the foot.

APL.clue: Thumb muscle in the first dorsal compartment, involved in de Quervain tenosynovitis along with extensor pollicis brevis
APL.rationale: It abducts the thumb and forms a radial border of the snuffbox. Pain is at the radial styloid, not in the carpal tunnel.

EPB.clue: Short thumb extensor that shares the first dorsal compartment with abductor pollicis longus
EPB.rationale: Both tendons are inflamed in de Quervain tenosynovitis. Extensor pollicis longus is in a separate compartment and forms the other snuffbox border.

VOLKMANN.clue: Ischemic flexion contracture of the forearm after untreated compartment syndrome or a supracondylar fracture
VOLKMANN.rationale: The brachial artery and median nerve are at risk with that fracture. Pain out of proportion and pain on passive finger extension are earlier warnings than a lost pulse.

PHRENIC.clue: Nerve from C3–C5 that innervates the diaphragm
PHRENIC.rationale: A cord injury at C1–C3 usually requires a ventilator, and C4 injuries often still need ventilatory support. Patients at C5 and below more often breathe without a ventilator but have a weak cough.

DIAPHRAGM.clue: Primary muscle of inspiration; it descends to increase thoracic volume and is innervated from C3 through C5
DIAPHRAGM.rationale: Paradoxical inward motion of the abdomen during inspiration means it is weak. Accessory muscles such as the scalenes and sternocleidomastoid then dominate.

SCALENE.clue: Neck muscles that elevate the first rib; the brachial plexus and subclavian artery pass between the anterior and middle ones
SCALENE.rationale: The subclavian vein passes in front of the anterior muscle, not through the triangle. Hypertrophy or an extra rib narrows the outlet.

TOS.clue: Compression of the brachial plexus or subclavian vessels at the scalenes, costoclavicular space, or pectoralis minor
TOS.rationale: Provocative positions reproduce arm heaviness or pulse change, but imaging or vascular studies are required before a structural diagnosis is firm.

PLEXUS.clue: Brachial network from C5–T1 arranged as roots, trunks, divisions, cords, and terminal nerves
PLEXUS.rationale: Upper trunk is C5–C6, middle is C7, and lower is C8–T1. The posterior cord gives the axillary and radial nerves; the lateral and medial cords both contribute to the median nerve.

KLUMPKE.clue: Lower-trunk palsy (C8–T1) with intrinsic-hand weakness and, if T1 sympathetics are involved, Horner syndrome
KLUMPKE.rationale: It follows traction with the arm overhead, including some birth injuries. The posture is a claw hand rather than a waiter's tip.

WAITER.clue: Tip posture of an upper-trunk (C5–C6) palsy: the shoulder is adducted and internally rotated, the elbow extended, and the forearm pronated
WAITER.rationale: Abduction, external rotation, and elbow flexion are lost. It is the Erb-Duchenne pattern, from birth traction or a blow that depresses the shoulder.

OBSTETRIC.clue: Brachial-plexus palsy from birth traction; an upper-trunk pattern presents with a waiter's-tip arm
OBSTETRIC.rationale: Most neurapraxia-level injuries recover, but a flaccid arm that is not improving needs specialty follow-up. Shoulder contracture and scapular winging are watched during recovery.

HORNER.clue: Triad of ptosis, miosis, and anhidrosis from interruption of sympathetic supply to the head
HORNER.rationale: In the neck and arm it can accompany a T1 lesion, a lower-trunk palsy, or an apical lung tumor. The pupil is small, not dilated.

PTOSIS.clue: Drooping eyelid; with a small pupil and loss of facial sweating it completes Horner syndrome
PTOSIS.rationale: Ptosis with a dilated pupil and an eye that sits down and out is instead an oculomotor-nerve lesion. The pupil finding separates the two.

MIOSIS.clue: Constricted pupil, one feature of interrupted sympathetic supply to the eye
MIOSIS.rationale: It is part of Horner syndrome. A dilated pupil that does not react to light fits an oculomotor lesion or pharmacologic block, not this finding.

ANHIDROSIS.clue: Loss of sweating on one side of the face, the autonomic part of Horner syndrome
ANHIDROSIS.rationale: It occurs when the sympathetic lesion is proximal to the carotid plexus split. Ptosis and miosis can be present without it if the lesion is more distal.

PANCOAST.clue: Tumor at the lung apex that can cause shoulder pain, intrinsic-hand weakness, and Horner syndrome
PANCOAST.rationale: The lower brachial plexus and the cervical sympathetic chain lie against the apex. Unexplained medial arm pain with a smoking history is not treated as a simple cervical strain.

STINGER.clue: Transient brachial-plexus traction injury in contact sports, with burning pain down one arm
STINGER.rationale: Symptoms should resolve within minutes. Persistent weakness, bilateral symptoms, or repeated events require a fuller neurologic workup before return to play.

FEMORAL.clue: Nerve from L2–L4 that innervates iliacus, sartorius, and the quadriceps and supplies sensation to the anterior thigh and medial leg
FEMORAL.rationale: A lesion weakens knee extension and reduces the patellar reflex. The saphenous nerve is its sensory continuation below the knee and has no motor fibers.

SAPHENOUS.clue: Sensory continuation of the femoral nerve along the medial leg, with no motor supply
SAPHENOUS.rationale: Compression causes medial knee or leg numbness without weakness. Quadriceps strength should be normal, which separates it from a femoral or L3–L4 lesion.

OBTURATOR.clue: Nerve from L2–L4 that innervates the hip adductors and gracilis and supplies a patch of medial thigh skin
OBTURATOR.rationale: A lesion weakens adduction and can follow pelvic surgery or obturator hernia. Hip adduction is spared in a femoral-nerve lesion.

MERALGIA.clue: Paresthetica: compression of the lateral femoral cutaneous nerve causing burning on the lateral thigh without weakness
MERALGIA.rationale: The nerve passes under the inguinal ligament and is compressed by tight belts, pregnancy, or prone surgical positioning. Hip-flexor strength is preserved, unlike an L2 root lesion.

SCIATIC.clue: Nerve from L4–S3 that innervates the hamstrings and then divides into tibial and common fibular nerves
SCIATIC.rationale: The short head of biceps femoris is the one hamstring innervated by the fibular division. Posterior hip dislocation and misplaced injections can injure the nerve.

PIRIFORMIS.clue: Hip external rotator, when the hip is extended, that the sciatic nerve may pass through or beneath
PIRIFORMIS.rationale: The flexion, adduction, and internal-rotation test is used to provoke buttock pain that radiates in a sciatic pattern. Hamstring or lumbar sources must be separated from it.

TIBIAL.clue: Nerve that plantarflexes the ankle and toes, inverts with tibialis posterior, and supplies the sole of the foot
TIBIAL.rationale: A lesion prevents heel rise and weakens inversion. It can be compressed behind the medial malleolus, causing burning on the sole.

TARSAL.clue: Tunnel behind the medial malleolus where the tibial nerve is compressed, causing burning on the sole
TARSAL.rationale: This is different from plantar heel pain that is worst with the first morning steps. A Tinel sign behind the malleolus supports the nerve site.

PERONEAL.clue: Common fibular nerve that winds the fibular head; compression causes foot drop and eversion weakness with inversion spared
PERONEAL.rationale: Inversion is spared because tibialis posterior is tibial-innervated. A deep-branch lesion weakens dorsiflexion only and changes sensation in the first web space.

SURAL.clue: Sensory nerve to the lateral foot, formed from tibial and fibular contributions, with no muscle supply
SURAL.rationale: It can be biopsied or irritated by a cast. Strength of plantarflexion and eversion should be normal in an isolated lesion.

PUDENDAL.clue: Nerve from S2–S4 that innervates the perineum and the external urethral and anal sphincters
PUDENDAL.rationale: Cyclists can compress it against the saddle. It is the nerve of pelvic-floor motor control and of genital sensation.

SUPERIOR.clue: Gluteal nerve from L4–S1 that innervates gluteus medius, gluteus minimus, and tensor fasciae latae
SUPERIOR.rationale: Injury produces a contralateral pelvic drop in single-leg stance. Intramuscular injection in the wrong quadrant of the buttock can hit it.

INFERIOR.clue: Gluteal nerve from L5–S2 that innervates gluteus maximus
INFERIOR.rationale: Weakness makes stair climbing and rising from a chair difficult and produces a posterior trunk lean in early stance. The abductors are spared.

GLUTEUS.clue: Medius keeps the opposite pelvis level in single-limb stance; maximus extends the hip in early stance
GLUTEUS.rationale: Medius and minimus are superior-gluteal; maximus is inferior-gluteal. Weak medius causes a Trendelenburg gait, and weak maximus causes a lurch of the trunk backward.

TENSOR.clue: Fasciae latae muscle that flexes, abducts, and internally rotates the hip and is innervated by the superior gluteal nerve
TENSOR.rationale: It tightens the iliotibial band. The modified Ober test with the knee extended biases length testing toward this muscle.

ILIOPSOAS.clue: Primary hip flexor; iliacus is femoral-innervated and psoas is innervated by lumbar ventral rami
ILIOPSOAS.rationale: It is the main muscle that advances the limb in initial swing. Tightness is seen when the opposite thigh lifts as one knee is hugged to the chest.

PSOAS.clue: Hip flexor from the lumbar spine, innervated by ventral rami rather than the femoral nerve
PSOAS.rationale: An abscess here can compress the femoral nerve or refer pain to the hip. It is a primary flexor together with iliacus.

SARTORIUS.clue: Femoral-innervated muscle that flexes, abducts, and externally rotates the hip and flexes the knee
SARTORIUS.rationale: It is the tailor's muscle and the longest muscle in the body. It forms the lateral border of the femoral triangle.

PECTINEUS.clue: Hip adductor and flexor innervated primarily by the femoral nerve
PECTINEUS.rationale: It forms part of the floor of the femoral triangle. Some people also receive a twig from the obturator nerve.

GRACILIS.clue: Obturator-innervated adductor that also flexes the knee and is the only adductor to cross it
GRACILIS.rationale: It is a common tendon graft. Medial knee pain at its insertion can mimic a medial collateral injury.

QUADRICEPS.clue: Knee extensors innervated by the femoral nerve; only rectus femoris also flexes the hip
QUADRICEPS.rationale: The patellar reflex screens L3–L4. Inhibition after knee surgery is common, so early activation is an explicit goal.

RECTUS.clue: Femoris: the only quadriceps muscle that crosses the hip, so it flexes the hip and extends the knee
RECTUS.rationale: In prone, bending the knee so the hip lifts indicates tightness. It is femoral-innervated, like the vasti.

VASTUS.clue: Medialis, lateralis, and intermedius: one-joint knee extensors innervated by the femoral nerve
VASTUS.rationale: They do not flex the hip. The oblique fibers of vastus medialis are not selectively strengthened by a short-arc quad.

VMO.clue: Oblique fibers of vastus medialis; they are not isolated by a terminal knee extension exercise
VMO.rationale: Patellofemoral programs train hip and knee control of the whole limb. These fibers are femoral-innervated and contribute to knee extension, not to a separate diagnosis by themselves.

HAMSTRING.clue: Group that decelerates the tibia at terminal swing and extends the hip in early stance
HAMSTRING.rationale: The tibial division of the sciatic nerve supplies all of the group except the short head of biceps femoris, which is common-fibular. Eccentric demand is highest at the end of swing.

POPLITEUS.clue: Tibial-innervated muscle that unlocks the knee by internally rotating the tibia at the start of flexion
POPLITEUS.rationale: In the open chain the tibia externally rotates in the last degrees of extension, the screw-home mechanism. This muscle reverses that rotation.

SCREW.clue: Home mechanism: the tibia externally rotates on the femur in the last degrees of open-chain extension
SCREW.rationale: In closed chain the femur internally rotates on a fixed tibia. Popliteus unlocks the knee to start flexion.

MENISCUS.clue: Fibrocartilage that deepens the knee; the medial one is less mobile and more often torn
MENISCUS.rationale: The outer third is vascular and may heal; the inner third is not. A repair, unlike a partial removal, usually limits deep flexion and weight bearing at first.

TRIAD.clue: Classic unhappy combination of anterior cruciate, medial collateral, and medial meniscus injury
TRIAD.rationale: The mechanism is a valgus and rotation force. Modern series sometimes find the lateral meniscus torn with the cruciate, but the classic trio is still the one taught for this name.

ACL.clue: Intra-articular ligament that limits anterior translation of the tibia and is the structure tested by the Lachman maneuver
ACL.rationale: Early rehabilitation emphasizes full passive extension and quadriceps activation. Resisted open-chain extension near full extension is limited at first because it shears the tibia forward.

PCL.clue: Intra-articular ligament that limits posterior translation of the tibia
PCL.rationale: A sag at 90 degrees of hip and knee flexion and a posterior drawer are the clinical tests. Dashboard trauma and a fall on a flexed knee are typical mechanisms.

MCL.clue: Medial knee ligament that resists valgus and has a deep attachment to the medial meniscus
MCL.rationale: It is tested at 30 degrees of flexion. Unlike the lateral collateral ligament, it is connected to the adjacent meniscus.

LCL.clue: Lateral knee ligament that resists varus and does not attach to the meniscus
LCL.rationale: It is tested at 30 degrees of flexion. Varus laxity at full extension implies injury beyond this ligament.

PATELLA.clue: Sesamoid in the quadriceps tendon that increases the moment arm of knee extension
PATELLA.rationale: A lateral push that reproduces fear of dislocation indicates insufficient medial restraints. Anterior knee pain after sitting is a separate, more common tracking problem.

ANGLE.clue: Formed by lines from the anterior superior iliac spine to the patella and from the patella to the tibial tubercle
ANGLE.rationale: A larger value increases the lateral pull on the patella and is typically greater in women because of a wider pelvis. It is only one factor in patellofemoral pain.

THEATER.clue: Sign of anterior knee pain after prolonged sitting that eases once the person walks
THEATER.rationale: It fits patellofemoral pain. Descending stairs, which loads the joint in flexion, is often more painful than ascending.

ILIOFEMORAL.clue: Y-shaped hip ligament that limits extension and external rotation and is the strongest ligament in the body
ILIOFEMORAL.rationale: It is a major static restraint in standing. The pubofemoral ligament limits abduction, and the ischiofemoral ligament limits internal rotation.

PUBOFEMORAL.clue: Hip ligament that primarily limits abduction and hyperextension
PUBOFEMORAL.rationale: It reinforces the inferior capsule. The Y ligament is the main check on extension; this one is the main check on abduction.

LIGAMENTUM.clue: Teres of the hip: a small intracapsular ligament that carries a vessel to the femoral head, more important in children
LIGAMENTUM.rationale: It is not a major stabilizer. The retinacular vessels from the medial femoral circumflex artery are the main adult supply to the head.

ACETABULUM.clue: Socket of the hip, deepened by the labrum, that faces laterally, inferiorly, and anteriorly
ACETABULUM.rationale: A shallow socket in an infant is developmental dysplasia. Femoroacetabular impingement pinches the labrum between the rim and the femoral neck.

LABRUM.clue: Fibrocartilage rim that deepens the glenoid or the acetabulum
LABRUM.rationale: A superior glenoid tear from anterior to posterior is a SLAP lesion. An anterior-inferior glenoid tear after dislocation is a Bankart lesion.

SLAP.clue: Superior labrum tear from anterior to posterior, often painful with biceps loading and overhead activity
SLAP.rationale: Peel-back in abduction and external rotation and traction on the biceps anchor are mechanisms. Early repair protocols limit resisted elbow flexion and supination.

BANKART.clue: Avulsion of the anterior-inferior glenoid labrum, associated with anterior shoulder dislocation
BANKART.rationale: Early repair protection limits external rotation and abduction, the position that stresses the anterior repair. A compression fracture of the posterolateral humeral head often accompanies the dislocation.

HILL.clue: Sachs lesion: a compression fracture of the posterolateral humeral head from anterior shoulder dislocation
HILL.rationale: The humeral head impacts the anterior glenoid rim. A large defect can make arthroscopic labral repair alone unstable.

LIGHTBULB.clue: Radiographic appearance of a posterior shoulder dislocation: the humeral head looks symmetric because the arm is locked in internal rotation
LIGHTBULB.rationale: Posterior dislocation follows seizures or electric shock and is missed on a single anteroposterior view. The arm is adducted and internally rotated, not held out to the side.

SEIZURE.clue: Neurologic event during which the head is protected, nothing is placed in the mouth, and emergency help is called if it lasts beyond about five minutes
SEIZURE.rationale: Afterward the person is placed on the side once convulsions stop. A posterior shoulder dislocation is a known complication of a major convulsion.

BURSA.clue: Fluid-filled sac that reduces friction; the one under the acromion is irritated in subacromial pain
BURSA.rationale: The olecranon, greater trochanter, and prepatellar sites are other common locations. A hot bursitis with fever is treated as possible infection.

TROCHANTER.clue: Lateral hip prominence where pain with side-lying and resisted abduction is often gluteal tendinopathy
TROCHANTER.rationale: The older label is bursitis, but the gluteus medius and minimus tendons are usually the painful tissue. Hip abductor loading is the basis of treatment.

ITB.clue: Thickened fascia from the iliac crest to Gerdy tubercle that can rub the lateral femoral condyle near 30 degrees of flexion
ITB.rationale: The Ober test assesses its length and the Noble test reproduces the friction pain. Hip abductor control is addressed along with the local irritation.

AVN.clue: Death of bone from lost blood supply, classically the femoral head after a displaced neck fracture or the proximal scaphoid
AVN.rationale: Steroids and alcohol are nontraumatic risks for the femoral head. Groin pain and limited hip internal rotation are the usual clinical picture.

LEGG.clue: Calvé-Perthes disease: idiopathic osteonecrosis of the femoral head in a child, usually a boy of about four to eight years
LEGG.rationale: Onset is gradual, with a limp and limited abduction and internal rotation. It is not the slipped epiphysis of an older, heavier adolescent.

SCFE.clue: Adolescent slip of the femoral head through the growth plate, often in an overweight child, and an urgent referral
SCFE.rationale: The hip rests in external rotation, flexion produces further external rotation, and knee pain may be the only complaint. Unstable slips are kept non-weight-bearing.

DDH.clue: Infant hip instability or a shallow socket, screened with Ortolani and Barlow maneuvers
DDH.rationale: With the hips and knees flexed, one knee sitting lower suggests dislocation on that side. An abduction orthosis holds the hips flexed and abducted, avoiding extreme abduction that can threaten the femoral head.

PAVLIK.clue: Harness that holds an infant's hips flexed and abducted for developmental dysplasia
PAVLIK.rationale: Excessive abduction is avoided because it can compromise blood flow to the femoral head. The family is taught skin checks and continuous wear as prescribed.

OSGOOD.clue: Schlatter disease: traction apophysitis of the tibial tubercle in growing adolescents
OSGOOD.rationale: Pain is at the tendon insertion and increases with jumping and kneeling. Activity is modified; the apophysis fuses and the pain resolves.

SEVER.clue: Disease: calcaneal apophysitis in active children, with posterior heel pain at the Achilles insertion
SEVER.rationale: Squeeze tenderness of the apophysis is typical. Heel cups, calf flexibility, and load reduction are used while growth cartilage is open.

SINDING.clue: Larsen-Johansson syndrome: apophysitis at the inferior pole of the patella in adolescents
SINDING.rationale: It is the patellar-pole counterpart of tibial-tubercle apophysitis and is related to repetitive jumping. Rest from painful loading is the main treatment.

APOPHYSIS.clue: Growth cartilage where a tendon attaches, the site of traction injuries such as Osgood-Schlatter disease
APOPHYSIS.rationale: Adolescents get pain at the insertion rather than in the mid-tendon. The cartilage fuses with maturity and the pain usually resolves.

SALTER.clue: Harris classification of growth-plate fractures; the type that crosses the physis and a corner of the metaphysis is the most common
SALTER.rationale: Type I is separation through the physis, type III enters the epiphysis, type IV crosses epiphysis and metaphysis, and type V is a crush. Growth arrest is the long-term concern.

GREENSTICK.clue: Incomplete fracture of a child's bone in which one cortex breaks and the other bends
GREENSTICK.rationale: The periosteum is thick and often stays intact on the concave side. It is distinct from a buckle, or torus, fracture in which the cortex only compresses.

TORUS.clue: Buckle fracture of a child's metaphysis in which the cortex compresses without a complete break
TORUS.rationale: It is usually stable. Point tenderness after a fall, especially of the distal radius, is the clue when deformity is minimal.

BLOUNT.clue: Disease of disordered medial proximal tibial growth that causes progressive bowing in a child
BLOUNT.rationale: It is distinguished from the mild bowing that is normal in infants and resolves. Asymmetry, a lateral thrust in stance, or worsening alignment prompts referral.

VALGUM.clue: Knock-knee alignment, a normal phase in early childhood
VALGUM.rationale: Asymmetry, pain, or persistence well past early childhood should be evaluated. In adults, this alignment loads the lateral compartment of the knee.

VARUM.clue: Bow-leg alignment, typical in infants and usually resolved by early childhood
VARUM.rationale: Pathologic causes include Blount disease and rickets. In older adults it loads the medial compartment and is common with medial osteoarthritis.

CLUBFOOT.clue: Equinovarus deformity: the foot points down and in, with forefoot adduction, treated by serial casting
CLUBFOOT.rationale: The Ponseti method uses weekly casts and often an Achilles tenotomy, then bracing to hold correction. It is not the flexible inward curve of the forefoot alone.

PONSETI.clue: Serial-casting method for clubfoot, usually followed by a heel-cord release and long-term bracing
PONSETI.rationale: Casts gradually correct cavus, adductus, and varus before equinus. Recurrence is the reason bracing continues after the foot looks corrected.

ADDUCTUS.clue: Forefoot that curves inward; a flexible curve can be stretched, and the hips should be checked for dysplasia
ADDUCTUS.rationale: The hindfoot is relatively neutral, unlike clubfoot. A rigid deformity needs referral rather than stretching alone.

TORTICOLLIS.clue: Infantile tightness of one sternocleidomastoid, tilting the head toward the tight side and rotating the face away
TORTICOLLIS.rationale: A tight right muscle produces right tilt and left rotation. Stretching, positioning, and tummy time are first-line, and plagiocephaly often coexists.

DOWN.clue: Syndrome with hypotonia, ligamentous laxity, and risk of atlantoaxial instability
DOWN.rationale: Forceful neck flexion, extension, and somersaults are avoided until the cervical spine is cleared. New neurologic signs such as gait change or urinary retention need urgent review.

BIFIDA.clue: Neural-tube defect; the myelomeningocele form leaves spinal cord and meninges exposed and causes paralysis below the lesion
BIFIDA.rationale: Hydrocephalus, a shunt, neurogenic bowel and bladder, and latex allergy are common. A change in strength, spasticity, or bladder function can signal a tethered cord.

MENINGOCELE.clue: Neural-tube defect in which meninges, but not the spinal cord, protrude
MENINGOCELE.rationale: Neurologic deficit is often mild compared with the form that includes neural tissue. Skin integrity over the sac and hydrocephalus are still monitored.

LATEX.clue: Allergy that is common in children with myelomeningocele; gloves and equipment in therapy should be free of it
LATEX.rationale: Repeated surgical and catheter exposure sensitizes these children. Balloons, elastic bands, and some exercise bands are hidden sources.

SHUNT.clue: Ventricular catheter, often to the peritoneum, used for hydrocephalus
SHUNT.rationale: Headache, vomiting, irritability, lethargy, or sunset eyes can signal malfunction and are an emergency. Therapy stops and the neurosurgery service is contacted.

DUCHENNE.clue: X-linked muscular dystrophy of boys with proximal weakness, calf pseudohypertrophy, and a waddling gait
DUCHENNE.rationale: The child walks the hands up the thighs to stand. High-resistance and eccentric exercise are avoided because they can accelerate muscle damage.

GOWERS.clue: Sign: a child with proximal weakness walks the hands up the thighs to rise from the floor
GOWERS.rationale: It is classic for Duchenne muscular dystrophy but occurs in any marked pelvic-girdle weakness. It is a compensation, not a primitive reflex.

MARFAN.clue: Connective-tissue disorder with tall stature, long fingers, lens dislocation, and risk of aortic aneurysm
MARFAN.rationale: Contact sports and maximal isometric straining are restricted because of the aorta. Scoliosis and joint laxity are common therapy concerns.

EHLERS.clue: Danlos syndromes: collagen disorders with joint hypermobility, fragile skin, and, in the vascular type, risk of arterial rupture
EHLERS.rationale: Therapy protects joints and avoids end-range stretching as an exercise. Sudden chest or abdominal pain is an emergency in the vascular type.

IMPERFECTA.clue: Osteogenesis type: brittle bones from a collagen defect, with fractures from minimal trauma
IMPERFECTA.rationale: Handling is gentle, rotational forces and high-impact activity are avoided, and aquatic exercise is often used. Blue sclerae are common but not present in every type.

PALSY.clue: Cerebral: a nonprogressive brain lesion causing disorders of movement and posture; musculoskeletal impairments can still worsen with growth
PALSY.rationale: Spastic diplegia affects the legs more than the arms and is linked to periventricular injury in premature infants. The brain lesion does not advance, but contracture and bony deformity can.

DIPLEGIA.clue: Cerebral palsy pattern with the legs more involved than the arms, often after periventricular injury in a premature infant
DIPLEGIA.rationale: Scissoring from adductor tone and an equinus or crouch pattern are common. Periventricular leukomalacia is the typical lesion.

PREMATURE.clue: Birth before term; periventricular white-matter injury in these infants is a common cause of spastic diplegia
PREMATURE.rationale: The white matter near the ventricles carries fibers to the legs. Tone, hip abduction, and motor milestones are followed closely.

HEMIPLEGIA.clue: Weakness of one side of the body, the pattern of many middle-cerebral-artery strokes and of one form of cerebral palsy
HEMIPLEGIA.rationale: The arm is often more involved than the leg in a cortical lesion. Gait may show equinus and circumduction of the weaker limb.

GMFCS.clue: Five-level system of gross motor function in cerebral palsy, from walking without limits to being transported in a wheelchair
GMFCS.rationale: Level I walks without limitations, level III walks with a handheld device, and level V is transported. The level describes function, not the quality of movement.

BOTULINUM.clue: Toxin injected into selected muscles to reduce focal spasticity for about three to four months
BOTULINUM.rationale: The window is used for stretching, orthoses, and practice of the desired movement. It does not replace a strengthening or task-specific program.

BACLOFEN.clue: Drug, given by mouth or into the spinal fluid, that reduces spasticity
BACLOFEN.rationale: Sudden withdrawal of the intrathecal form is an emergency and can cause rebound spasticity, fever, itching, hallucinations, and seizures. A pump alarm or a sudden tone increase is reported immediately.

PHENOL.clue: Injection at a motor point or nerve used for a longer reduction of spasticity than botulinum toxin
PHENOL.rationale: Effects can last many months. If a mixed nerve is injected, painful dysesthesias can follow, so motor-point technique is preferred in a sensory nerve.

SERIAL.clue: Casting that uses successive casts to gain range in a contracture or a spastic limb
SERIAL.rationale: Each cast holds a low-load stretch, and casts are changed as range improves. Skin is checked at every change.

CONTRACTURE.clue: Fixed shortening of muscle or joint tissue that limits range even when the stretch is slow
CONTRACTURE.rationale: Spasticity, by contrast, depends on speed. Slow passive range that still stops early is this structural limit, not a reflex catch.

TONE.clue: Resistance of resting muscle to passive stretch, assessed slowly so a contracture is not mistaken for a reflex
TONE.rationale: Velocity-dependent catch is spasticity from an upper motor neuron lesion. Resistance that is the same at slow and fast speed is rigidity or a soft-tissue limit.

SPASTICITY.clue: Velocity-dependent increase in stretch-reflex resistance from an upper motor neuron lesion
SPASTICITY.rationale: It is not rigidity, which resists both directions at any speed. Fast stretch increases the catch; a slow stretch better shows the available range.

RIGIDITY.clue: Velocity-independent resistance in both directions, typical of Parkinson disease
RIGIDITY.rationale: Lead-pipe resistance is smooth, and cogwheel resistance is the same stiffness with a tremor superimposed. Stretch speed does not change it the way it changes spasticity.

COGWHEEL.clue: Ratchet resistance felt when tremor is superimposed on lead-pipe stiffness in Parkinson disease
COGWHEEL.rationale: It is most evident during slow passive motion of the wrist or elbow. It is a basal-ganglia sign, not a cerebellar one.

FLACCID.clue: Abnormally low tone with little resistance to passive stretch
FLACCID.rationale: It occurs with lower motor neuron lesions and during spinal shock or the first stage after some strokes. Reflexes are reduced or absent, and atrophy follows denervation.

CLASP.clue: Knife response: a catch during passive stretch of a spastic muscle followed by a sudden giving way
CLASP.rationale: It is an upper motor neuron release phenomenon. The catch is velocity sensitive, which separates it from the uniform resistance of rigidity.

UMN.clue: Lesion pattern of spasticity, hyperreflexia, and an extensor plantar response, without fasciculations
