UMN.rationale: Acute spinal shock is the exception and is temporarily flaccid. Muscle bulk is relatively preserved compared with a lower motor neuron lesion.

LMN.clue: Lesion pattern of flaccid weakness, hyporeflexia, fasciculations, and marked atrophy
LMN.rationale: The lesion is in the anterior horn, root, plexus, or peripheral nerve. Plantar responses are not extensor from this lesion alone.

DTR.clue: Deep tendon reflex graded from 0 (absent) to 4+ (with clonus); 2+ is normal
DTR.rationale: Biceps screens C5–C6, triceps C7, the patellar reflex L3–L4, and the Achilles reflex S1–S2. A reflex that is hard to elicit can be reinforced by having the patient pull the hooked fingers apart.

MYOTOME.clue: Muscles served by one spinal nerve; key screens include shoulder abduction C5, wrist extension C6, elbow extension C7, ankle dorsiflexion L4, great-toe extension L5, and ankle plantarflexion S1
MYOTOME.rationale: The spinal-cord injury motor exam uses elbow flexion C5, wrist extension C6, elbow extension C7, finger flexion C8, finger abduction T1, hip flexion L2, knee extension L3, ankle dorsiflexion L4, long-toe extension L5, and ankle plantarflexion S1.

DERMATOME.clue: Skin region supplied by one nerve root; C6 is the thumb, C7 the middle finger, C8 the little finger, T4 the nipple, T10 the umbilicus, L4 the medial malleolus, L5 the dorsum of the foot, and S1 the lateral foot
DERMATOME.rationale: A band of sensory change matching one of these regions supports radiculopathy. Stocking-glove loss instead suggests a polyneuropathy.

REFLEX.clue: Involuntary motor response; biceps tests C5–C6, triceps C7, quadriceps L3–L4, and the Achilles tendon S1–S2
REFLEX.rationale: Grades run from absent to sustained clonus. An extensor plantar response and clonus support an upper motor neuron lesion, while loss of the reflex supports a root or peripheral lesion.

FASCICLE.clue: Visible twitch of a motor unit, a lower-motor-neuron sign when widespread
FASCICLE.rationale: Fibrillation, by contrast, is a single denervated fiber seen only on electromyography. Both point to axonal or anterior-horn injury rather than an upper motor neuron lesion.

WALLERIAN.clue: Degeneration of the axon distal to a transection; the distal segment dies and regrowth must come from the proximal stump
WALLERIAN.rationale: Conduction in the distal stump fails over several days. Regeneration, when the sheath is intact, proceeds at about 1 mm per day after a short latency.

NEURAPRAXIA.clue: Mildest nerve injury: conduction is blocked but the axon is intact, so Wallerian degeneration does not occur
NEURAPRAXIA.rationale: Recovery is expected over days to weeks as myelin is restored. Saturday-night radial palsy and many compression injuries are this grade.

AXONOTMESIS.clue: Nerve injury in which the axon is cut but the connective-tissue sheath remains, allowing regeneration of about 1 mm per day
AXONOTMESIS.rationale: The distal axon undergoes Wallerian degeneration. Prognosis is good if the endoneurial tube is intact, but recovery time depends on the distance to the muscle.

NEUROTMESIS.clue: Complete disruption of a nerve including its sheath; spontaneous recovery is poor without surgical repair
NEUROTMESIS.rationale: It is the most severe Seddon grade. Even after repair, misrouting of axons can limit function.

SUNDERLAND.clue: Five-degree classification of nerve injury, from conduction block to complete transection
SUNDERLAND.rationale: First degree matches neurapraxia and fifth degree matches a severed nerve. The middle degrees describe increasing damage to the connective-tissue layers.

EMG.clue: Needle study of muscle electrical activity; fibrillation potentials after denervation appear over the following weeks, not on the day of injury
EMG.rationale: A study done too early can look normal despite a real axonal injury. Fasciculation potentials are motor-unit discharges and can be seen clinically.

NCV.clue: Study of speed and size of a nerve's electrical response
NCV.rationale: Demyelination slows velocity or blocks conduction. Axonal loss mainly reduces amplitude while velocity stays relatively preserved.

MYELIN.clue: Sheath whose loss slows nerve conduction, as in Guillain-Barré syndrome
MYELIN.rationale: Conduction block and prolonged latency are the electrical findings. Axonal neuropathies instead shrink the size of the response.

GUILLAIN.clue: Barré syndrome: acute demyelinating polyneuropathy, often after infection, with ascending weakness and areflexia
GUILLAIN.rationale: Respiratory failure and autonomic instability are the dangers. Overwork can worsen weakness, so exercise stays submaximal and is stopped if the patient is weaker the next day.

ASCENDING.clue: Pattern of weakness in Guillain-Barré syndrome, starting in the legs and moving upward
ASCENDING.rationale: Respiratory muscles can be involved, so vital capacity and cough are monitored. Recovery often returns from the trunk toward the hands and feet.

PROXIMAL.clue: Direction toward the trunk; strength in Guillain-Barré often returns from the trunk outward
PROXIMAL.rationale: A lesion is also described by how close it is to the cell body. Hip and shoulder girdle weakness, as in muscular dystrophy, is named for this distribution.

DISTAL.clue: Direction away from the trunk; sensory loss of a polyneuropathy begins in the feet and hands in a stocking-glove pattern
DISTAL.rationale: Length-dependent neuropathies affect the longest axons first. This pattern is different from a single dermatome or a single peripheral nerve.

ALS.clue: Motor neuron disease affecting upper and lower motor neurons together, with spasticity, fasciculations, and spared sensation
ALS.rationale: Bulbar onset threatens speech and swallowing early. Exercise is moderate and stopped before overwork; respiratory decline is the usual cause of death.

BULBAR.clue: Onset of motor neuron disease that affects speech and swallowing before the limbs
BULBAR.rationale: Aspiration and respiratory failure occur earlier than in limb-onset disease. Fatigue of speech during a session is a practical warning.

MYASTHENIA.clue: Gravis: fatigable weakness that worsens with repetition and improves with rest, often with ptosis and diplopia
MYASTHENIA.rationale: Therapy is scheduled at peak medication effect and stops before muscles fail, because a respiratory crisis is a medical emergency. Lambert-Eaton syndrome, by contrast, can improve briefly after repeated contraction.

LAMBERT.clue: Eaton syndrome: weakness, often of the proximal legs, that can improve briefly with repetition and is associated with small-cell lung cancer
LAMBERT.rationale: It is the electrical and clinical opposite of myasthenia gravis, which fatigues with repetition. Autonomic symptoms such as dry mouth are common.

SCLEROSIS.clue: Multiple: central demyelination separated in time and space; heat can temporarily worsen symptoms
SCLEROSIS.rationale: Fatigue, optic neuritis, spasticity, and sensory change are common. Exercise is kept submaximal and cool, because a rise in temperature can transiently worsen conduction.

UHTHOFF.clue: Phenomenon: a temporary worsening of neurologic symptoms when body temperature rises in multiple sclerosis
UHTHOFF.rationale: Hot pools, fever, and overexertion can bring it on. Cooling and rest reverse it; it is not a new permanent lesion by itself.

OPTIC.clue: Neuritis: painful loss of vision in one eye, a common presentation of multiple sclerosis
OPTIC.rationale: A relative afferent pupillary defect may be present. The swinging-light test shows the affected pupil appearing to dilate when the light moves to that eye.

AFFERENT.clue: Pupillary defect: when the light swings to the affected eye, that pupil dilates, indicating an optic-nerve lesion
AFFERENT.rationale: Both pupils constrict when the light is on the good eye because the oculomotor output is intact. The defect is in the sensory limb, not the motor pupil pathway.

OXYGEN.clue: Supplemental gas prescribed to a saturation target; excess flow in some chronic retainers can raise carbon dioxide
OXYGEN.rationale: Nasal cannula flow raises inspired concentration by about 4 percent per liter, from about 24 percent at 1 liter. A Venturi mask gives a more precise dose when that control matters.

SATURATION.clue: Percent of hemoglobin bound with oxygen, estimated by pulse oximetry
SATURATION.rationale: Exercise is often paused below about 88 to 90 percent, or at the threshold in the order. Poor perfusion and dark nail polish make the finger reading unreliable.

CANNULA.clue: Low-flow device in the nose; each added liter per minute raises inspired oxygen by about 4 percent
CANNULA.rationale: One liter is about 24 percent and six liters about 44 percent. It does not deliver a fixed concentration when the patient breathes faster.

VENTURI.clue: Mask that delivers a set oxygen concentration and is preferred when carbon-dioxide retention requires a controlled dose
VENTURI.rationale: Color-coded jets set the air-to-oxygen mix. It is chosen over simply turning up a nasal cannula in a patient who retains carbon dioxide.

PURSED.clue: Lip breathing that slows exhalation and limits airway collapse in obstructive disease
PURSED.rationale: The patient inhales through the nose and exhales slowly through partly closed lips. It reduces respiratory rate and helps empty trapped air.

HUFF.clue: Open-glottis forced expiration that moves secretions without the high pressure of a closed-glottis cough
HUFF.rationale: It is useful when a cough causes bronchospasm or exhausts the patient. A cough can follow to clear secretions that reached larger airways.

COUGH.clue: Airway-clearance effort; when abdominal muscles are paralyzed, a manual upward thrust timed with the effort replaces them
COUGH.rationale: The assist is coordinated with the patient's attempt. A weak, wet cough after spinal cord injury is a reason to teach this technique.

INCENTIVE.clue: Spirometry that coaches a slow deep inhalation and a breath hold to reopen alveoli after surgery
INCENTIVE.rationale: It prevents atelectasis but does not replace walking. The patient inspires maximally rather than blowing out.

SPIROMETRY.clue: Pulmonary function test; an FEV1/FVC below 0.70 supports obstruction, while reduced volumes with a preserved ratio suggest restriction
SPIROMETRY.rationale: Simple spirometry cannot measure residual volume, so total lung capacity needs another method. Restriction is confirmed by a low total lung capacity.

OBSTRUCTIVE.clue: Lung-disease pattern with a reduced FEV1/FVC, air trapping, and a high residual volume
OBSTRUCTIVE.rationale: Emphysema, chronic bronchitis, and asthma are the main examples. Patients often breathe with pursed lips and a prolonged expiratory phase.

RESTRICTIVE.clue: Lung-disease pattern with reduced volumes and a normal or high FEV1/FVC
RESTRICTIVE.rationale: Fibrosis, kyphoscoliosis, and neuromuscular weakness are causes. The lung is small rather than obstructed, so the ratio does not fall.

EMPHYSEMA.clue: Obstructive disease with destroyed alveolar walls, air trapping, and a barreled chest
EMPHYSEMA.rationale: The classic thin, dyspneic presentation is the pink puffer. Pursed-lip breathing and paced activity are central to therapy.

BRONCHITIS.clue: Chronic form is defined by a productive cough for at least three months in two consecutive years
BRONCHITIS.rationale: It is an obstructive disease. The classic edematous, cyanotic presentation is the blue bloater, often with cor pulmonale.

ASTHMA.clue: Reversible airway obstruction with wheeze and dyspnea; a rescue inhaler should be available during exercise
ASTHMA.rationale: Known triggers are avoided. A peak-flow drop or increasing wheeze is a reason to stop and follow the patient's action plan.

WHEEZE.clue: Continuous musical lung sound from narrowed airways
WHEEZE.rationale: It is typical of asthma and other obstructive disease. Unlike crackles, it is continuous and may be heard in expiration or both phases.

CRACKLES.clue: Discontinuous lung sounds from fluid or atelectasis; bibasilar ones are common in left-sided heart failure
CRACKLES.rationale: They do not clear as reliably with a cough as secretions in larger airways. New crackles plus weight gain suggest worsening pulmonary edema.

RHONCHI.clue: Low-pitched continuous sounds that may clear with coughing, associated with secretions in larger airways
RHONCHI.rationale: They differ from fine crackles of fluid in small airways. Airway-clearance techniques are aimed at the secretions that produce them.

STRIDOR.clue: High-pitched inspiratory sound from upper-airway obstruction
STRIDOR.rationale: Severe stridor is an emergency. It is not the expiratory musical sound of lower-airway narrowing.

FREMITUS.clue: Tactile vibration of the voice; it increases over consolidation and decreases over effusion or pneumothorax
FREMITUS.rationale: The patient says a resonant phrase while the therapist palpates the chest. Percussion and breath sounds are interpreted with it.

EGOPHONY.clue: An E-to-A change heard over consolidated lung
EGOPHONY.rationale: It accompanies increased voice transmission, dull percussion, and crackles. Effusion and pneumothorax decrease voice transmission instead.

PERCUSSION.clue: Chest technique whose note becomes dull over fluid or consolidation and hyperresonant over trapped air or pneumothorax
PERCUSSION.rationale: A large area of collapse pulls the trachea toward that side. A large effusion or tension pneumothorax pushes the trachea away.

DULLNESS.clue: Percussion note over consolidation or pleural fluid
DULLNESS.rationale: Consolidation also increases fremitus, while effusion decreases it. The distinction uses voice transmission, not the note alone.

TRACHEA.clue: Airway whose shift toward one side suggests volume loss there, and whose shift away suggests a large effusion or air under pressure on the opposite side
TRACHEA.rationale: Atelectasis pulls, while pleural effusion and tension pneumothorax push. The finding is combined with breath sounds and percussion.

ATELECTASIS.clue: Collapse of alveoli that reduces breath sounds and, if large, pulls the trachea toward the affected side
ATELECTASIS.rationale: Incentive spirometry, mobilization, and deep breathing are used after surgery to prevent it. It is not the same as air in the pleural space, which pushes the trachea away.

PLEURAL.clue: Effusion: fluid around the lung that dulls percussion, decreases breath sounds, and can push the trachea away if large
PLEURAL.rationale: Fremitus is decreased. Drainage position and deep breathing do not replace treatment of the cause.

BARREL.clue: Chest shape of hyperinflation, with an increased anterior-posterior diameter, classic in emphysema
BARREL.rationale: The diaphragm is flattened and less efficient. Patients often lean forward on the hands to use accessory muscles.

TRIPOD.clue: Sitting posture of leaning forward on the hands, used to improve diaphragmatic mechanics in obstructive disease
TRIPOD.rationale: It fixes the shoulder girdle so accessory muscles can lift the chest. It is a sign of distress, not a stretching exercise.

PUFFER.clue: Classic thin, dyspneic presentation of emphysema, contrasted with the cyanotic, edematous chronic-bronchitis presentation
PUFFER.rationale: Patients use pursed lips and accessory muscles. The phenotypes overlap in real disease, but the contrast is still used to organize findings.

BLOATER.clue: Classic cyanotic, heavier presentation of chronic bronchitis with edema from right-heart strain
BLOATER.rationale: Chronic hypoxemia leads to pulmonary hypertension and cor pulmonale. Airway clearance and oxygen to the prescribed target are priorities.

CLUBBING.clue: Bulbous enlargement of the distal digits associated with long-standing hypoxemia
CLUBBING.rationale: It develops over time in chronic lung or heart disease. New clubbing with a cough needs medical evaluation rather than a joint diagnosis.

CYANOSIS.clue: Bluish color from hypoxemia; central involvement of the lips and tongue is more ominous than cool, peripheral color alone
CYANOSIS.rationale: Peripheral color can come from cold or poor circulation with a normal saturation. Central color means the arterial blood itself is poorly oxygenated.

ORTHOPNEA.clue: Dyspnea when lying flat, typical of left-sided heart failure
ORTHOPNEA.rationale: Ask how many pillows the patient uses. Sitting up reduces venous return to the lungs and eases the symptom.

DYSPNEA.clue: Shortness of breath; scales and the ability to talk are used to judge whether exercise intensity is appropriate
DYSPNEA.rationale: New or disproportionate dyspnea during cardiac or pulmonary exercise is a reason to stop. A modified 0-to-10 scale is often used.

PND.clue: Sudden nighttime shortness of breath that wakes the patient, classically in left-sided heart failure
PND.rationale: It is different from dyspnea that is present whenever the patient lies flat. Both point to pulmonary congestion.

EDEMA.clue: Palpable swelling from excess interstitial fluid; dependent pitting is common in right-sided heart failure
EDEMA.rationale: Daily weight is a better tracker than the look of the ankles alone. A gain of about 2 to 3 pounds in a day, or 5 in a week, should be reported.

WEIGHT.clue: A gain of about 2 to 3 pounds in a day or 5 pounds in a week can signal worsening heart failure
WEIGHT.rationale: Patients are taught to weigh themselves daily. A sudden gain with more pillows or new swelling is reported rather than exercised through.

JUGULAR.clue: Venous distention in the neck that indicates elevated right-sided filling pressure
JUGULAR.rationale: It is inspected with the head of the bed elevated. It accompanies edema and hepatic congestion in right-sided failure and cor pulmonale.

PULMONALE.clue: Right-sided heart failure caused by lung disease and pulmonary hypertension
PULMONALE.rationale: Edema, jugular distention, and dyspnea are the picture. Treating the lung disease and avoiding hypoxemia are the priorities.

GALLOP.clue: Extra heart sound; a third sound early in diastole can indicate heart failure, and a fourth suggests a stiff ventricle
GALLOP.rationale: The third sound is heard just after the second. New gallops during an exercise session are reported, especially with dyspnea.

PRELOAD.clue: End-diastolic stretch of the ventricle, raised by greater venous return
PRELOAD.rationale: Up to a point, more stretch produces a stronger contraction. In failure the ventricle is overstretched and further volume worsens congestion.

AFTERLOAD.clue: Resistance the ventricle must overcome to eject; systemic vascular resistance is the main left-sided contributor
AFTERLOAD.rationale: High blood pressure raises it and increases myocardial work. Vasodilator drugs lower it.

STARLING.clue: Law that a greater end-diastolic stretch produces a stronger beat, until the ventricle is overstretched in failure
STARLING.rationale: Exercise training can increase stroke volume partly through a larger filling volume. Failure sits on the flat part of the curve.

FRACTION.clue: Share of ventricular end-diastolic volume pumped in one beat, normally about 55 to 70 percent
FRACTION.rationale: Reduced systolic heart failure is generally at or below 40 percent. A preserved value can still cause failure if the ventricle fills poorly.

SYSTOLE.clue: Phase of the cardiac cycle when the ventricles contract and eject
SYSTOLE.rationale: The first heart sound marks the start. The left ventricular myocardium is perfused mainly in the next phase, not during ejection.

DIASTOLE.clue: Phase when the ventricles relax and fill; left-ventricular coronary flow occurs mainly then
DIASTOLE.rationale: A fast heart rate shortens this phase and can worsen ischemia. The second heart sound marks its start.

SINOATRIAL.clue: Node in the right atrium that normally paces the heart at about 60 to 100 beats per minute
SINOATRIAL.rationale: If it fails, the atrioventricular junction paces at about 40 to 60, and the Purkinje fibers of the ventricles pace at about 20 to 40. Slower escape rhythms are less reliable.

QRS.clue: Complex on the electrocardiogram that represents ventricular depolarization
QRS.rationale: It should be narrow when the impulse uses the normal conduction system. A wide, early complex without a P wave is a premature ventricular beat.

WENCKEBACH.clue: Second-degree atrioventricular block in which the PR interval lengthens until a QRS complex is dropped
WENCKEBACH.rationale: This type I pattern is often stable. Type II drops beats without progressive lengthening and is more dangerous.

COMPLETE.clue: Heart block with no relationship between P waves and QRS complexes, the ventricles running on an escape rhythm
COMPLETE.rationale: Symptomatic patients need urgent care. Exercise is not continued when this rhythm appears.

PVC.clue: Early wide QRS without a P wave; couplets, increasing frequency, or a run of three or more is a reason to stop exercise
PVC.rationale: One isolated beat in a stable patient may be tolerated. Three or more in a row is ventricular tachycardia.

BIGEMINY.clue: Pattern of one normal beat alternating with one premature ventricular beat
BIGEMINY.rationale: It is a reason to stop exercise and notify medical staff when it is new. Every other beat is ventricular.

TRIGEMINY.clue: Pattern in which every third beat is a premature ventricular complex
TRIGEMINY.rationale: Like couplets, new ventricular patterns during exercise are not pushed through. The session stops and the rhythm is reported.

COUPLET.clue: Two premature ventricular beats in a row; three or more is ventricular tachycardia
COUPLET.rationale: New couplets during exercise are an indication to stop. They imply a more irritable ventricle than a single isolated beat.

ISCHEMIA.clue: Imbalance of myocardial oxygen supply and demand; flat or downsloping ST depression of about 1 mm during exercise is a warning
ISCHEMIA.rationale: Angina, undue dyspnea, or that ST change stops the session. Demand is estimated clinically by heart rate times systolic pressure.

INFARCT.clue: Death of myocardium; ST-segment elevation is treated as acute injury and exercise is not continued
INFARCT.rationale: Cardiac rehabilitation begins only after the patient is medically stable. Chest pain that does not settle with rest and prescribed nitroglycerin activates emergency services.

ANGINA.clue: Myocardial ischemic pain, often pressure, provoked by exertion and relieved by rest or nitroglycerin
ANGINA.rationale: Stop activity and have the patient sit. If prescribed nitroglycerin does not relieve pain after the usual repeated doses, emergency services are activated.

NITRO.clue: Glycerin: a vasodilator for angina that can drop blood pressure, so the patient should sit before taking it
NITRO.rationale: Up to three doses about five minutes apart are a common plan. Unrelieved pain after that is treated as a possible infarction.

AFIB.clue: Irregularly irregular rhythm with no effective atrial contraction
AFIB.rationale: Rate control and anticoagulation status are confirmed before vigorous exercise. Some beats may not produce a radial pulse, so the apex is counted for a full minute.

DEFICIT.clue: Gap between a higher apical rate and a lower radial rate when some beats do not reach the wrist
DEFICIT.rationale: It occurs in atrial fibrillation. The apical count is the one used for decisions.

APICAL.clue: Pulse heard at the fifth intercostal space, midclavicular line, counted a full minute when the rhythm is irregular
APICAL.rationale: A radial count can miss beats that do not perfuse. The point of maximal impulse is the usual site.

CAROTID.clue: Artery palpated on one side at a time; pressure on both can slow the heart and reduce brain blood flow
CAROTID.rationale: Vigorous massage is not a therapy technique. A bruit or known carotid disease is a reason to use another pulse site.

CUFF.clue: Bladder that is too narrow for the arm gives a falsely high blood pressure
CUFF.rationale: The bladder should encircle most of the arm, and the width should be about 40 percent of the arm circumference. A cuff that is too wide reads low.

KOROTKOFF.clue: Sounds heard as a blood-pressure cuff deflates; the first is systolic and the disappearance is diastolic in adults
KOROTKOFF.rationale: The cuff is inflated above the expected systolic pressure and lowered about 2 mm Hg per second. Children sometimes use the muffling point rather than disappearance.

SYSTOLIC.clue: Blood pressure at the first Korotkoff sound; a drop of more than about 10 mm Hg as workload rises is a reason to stop
SYSTOLIC.rationale: A rise above about 250 mm Hg is also a standard stop criterion. The product of this pressure and heart rate indexes myocardial oxygen demand.

DIASTOLIC.clue: Blood pressure at the disappearance of Korotkoff sounds; a rise above about 115 mm Hg during exercise is a reason to stop
DIASTOLIC.rationale: It is the pressure in the arteries while the heart is filling. A falling systolic pressure with a rising diastolic pressure narrows pulse pressure and is a poor sign.

RPP.clue: Product of heart rate and systolic blood pressure, a clinical index of myocardial oxygen demand
RPP.rationale: Angina often appears at a repeatable value. Beta blockers lower the heart-rate contribution, so the same workload costs less.

KARVONEN.clue: Heart-rate reserve method: target rate equals resting rate plus a percentage of the difference between maximal and resting rates
KARVONEN.rationale: The formula is not valid if it was calculated without the drugs the patient actually takes. Beta blockers blunt the rise, so perceived exertion is used instead.

BLOCKER.clue: Beta drug that limits the rise in heart rate, so a target heart rate is a poor intensity guide
BLOCKER.rationale: Perceived exertion or a talk test is used. Nonselective agents can also provoke bronchospasm in asthma.

BORG.clue: Rating of perceived exertion; the original scale runs from 6 to 20 so the number roughly tracks heart rate times 10
BORG.rationale: A 0-to-10 category-ratio scale is used for dyspnea and for patients on heart-rate-limiting drugs. Moderate work is around 12 to 13 on the 6-to-20 scale.

RPE.clue: Perceived-exertion rating used to set intensity when heart rate is blunted by medicine or by a pacemaker
RPE.rationale: The patient is taught the anchors, from rest to maximal. Cardiac sessions often stay at or below somewhat hard.

MET.clue: Unit of oxygen cost equal to about 3.5 mL per kilogram per minute at rest
MET.rationale: Activity intensity is prescribed as multiples of rest. Light daily tasks are only a few multiples; a flight of stairs is often treated as a higher early goal after a cardiac event.

FITT.clue: Principle of exercise prescription: frequency, intensity, time, and type are each specified
FITT.rationale: Changing one variable at a time makes the dose clear. Intensity in cardiac disease is often set by perceived exertion rather than by an age-predicted heart rate.

TALK.clue: Test of aerobic intensity: speaking in sentences suggests moderate work, and being unable to speak suggests the work is too hard
TALK.rationale: It is useful when heart-rate formulas are unreliable. The patient should still be able to talk during many endurance sessions.

VALSALVA.clue: Forced expiration against a closed glottis that spikes blood pressure and is avoided by cardiac patients during lifts
VALSALVA.rationale: Exhale during the effort. The maneuver also raises intradiscal pressure, so breath-holding is discouraged with back pain.

ORTHOSTATIC.clue: Drop in systolic pressure of at least 20 mm Hg, or diastolic of at least 10, within three minutes of standing
ORTHOSTATIC.rationale: The patient is laid down if dizzy; this is the opposite of autonomic dysreflexia, where pressure is high and the patient is sat up. Slow rises, compression, and ankle pumps help.

HYPOTENSION.clue: Abnormally low blood pressure with dizziness or faintness, treated by lying the patient down and raising the legs
HYPOTENSION.rationale: It can follow abrupt stopping of exercise because blood pools in the legs. A cool-down keeps the muscle pump working.

POOLING.clue: Collection of blood in the legs if exercise stops abruptly; a gradual cool-down prevents a drop in pressure
POOLING.rationale: Cardiac patients are especially vulnerable. Walking slowly or ankle pumps are continued rather than sitting immediately.

TACHYCARDIA.clue: Resting heart rate above 100 beats per minute in an adult
TACHYCARDIA.rationale: It shortens diastole and can worsen ischemia. A new unexplained rise is assessed before exercise continues.

BRADYCARDIA.clue: Resting heart rate below 60 beats per minute in an adult
BRADYCARDIA.rationale: It may be normal in a trained person or caused by drugs or heart block. Symptoms, blood pressure, and the rhythm decide whether activity is safe.

TACHYPNEA.clue: Respiratory rate above 20 breaths per minute in a resting adult
TACHYPNEA.rationale: It is a sign of distress, fever, or cardiopulmonary disease. Exercise is not progressed while the resting rate is climbing.

BRADYPNEA.clue: Respiratory rate below 12 breaths per minute in a resting adult
BRADYPNEA.rationale: Sedation, neurologic injury, and fatigue of respiratory muscles are causes. A falling rate with a rising carbon dioxide is a reason for urgent support.

CHEYNE.clue: Stokes respiration: cycles of increasing then decreasing depth followed by apnea, seen in serious neurologic or cardiac illness
CHEYNE.rationale: The pattern is regular in its rise and fall. It is different from the irregular gasps of a brainstem lesion.

KUSSMAUL.clue: Deep, labored breathing of metabolic acidosis, as in diabetic ketoacidosis
KUSSMAUL.rationale: Fruity breath and a high glucose accompany it. Exercise is contraindicated and the patient needs urgent care.

BIOT.clue: Irregular breathing with unpredictable depth and periods of apnea, associated with a medullary lesion
BIOT.rationale: It lacks the smooth crescendo of Cheyne-Stokes breathing. It is a sign of brainstem dysfunction.

APNEUSTIC.clue: Prolonged inspiratory pauses associated with a pontine lesion
APNEUSTIC.rationale: The patient seems to hold each inspiration. It is a central pattern, not an obstructive one.

NEWBORN.clue: Normal heart rate is about 120 to 160 beats per minute and respiratory rate about 30 to 60, both much higher than in adults
NEWBORN.rationale: Adult norms of 60 to 100 and 12 to 20 do not apply. A slow rate in an infant is more concerning than the same number in an adult.

ABG.clue: Arterial blood sample that reports oxygen, carbon dioxide, and pH
ABG.rationale: Pulse oximetry does not show carbon dioxide. A rising carbon dioxide with a falling pH means ventilation is failing.

ECG.clue: Tracing of the heart's electrical activity; ST depression with effort can indicate ischemia and ST elevation can indicate acute injury
ECG.rationale: A widening QRS or a run of ventricular beats stops exercise. The tracing is interpreted with symptoms, not alone.

CHF.clue: Syndrome in which the heart does not meet demand; left-sided failure congests the lungs and right-sided failure causes edema and neck-vein distention
CHF.rationale: Exercise is low to moderate, with perceived exertion and a daily weight. Sudden gain, new nocturnal dyspnea, or increasing crackles are reported.

COPD.clue: Group of obstructive lung diseases, mainly emphysema and chronic bronchitis
COPD.rationale: Therapy uses airway clearance, pursed-lip breathing, paced activity, and endurance training. Oxygen is given to the prescribed saturation, not maximized by default.

CAD.clue: Narrowing of coronary arteries that produces angina when demand exceeds supply
CAD.rationale: Exercise stops for angina, undue dyspnea, or a falling systolic pressure. Training can raise the workload at which angina appears.

CABG.clue: Surgery that bypasses a coronary blockage with a vessel graft; sternal precautions apply when the sternum was divided
CABG.rationale: Traditional limits restrict lifting, pushing, and wide arm motion for the early weeks. Many centers now allow more motion inside a pain-free tube; the surgeon's protocol is followed.

STERNAL.clue: Precautions after median sternotomy that traditionally limit lifting, pushing, and reaching both arms overhead while the bone heals
STERNAL.rationale: A pillow splint is used for coughing. Protocols are becoming less restrictive, but early unprotected pushing and heavy lifting are still avoided.

ANGIOPLASTY.clue: Procedure that opens a coronary artery through a peripheral puncture
ANGIOPLASTY.rationale: After femoral access, a growing groin hematoma, back or flank pain, or a drop in blood pressure can signal bleeding. There is no sternal wound unless a bypass was also done.

PACEMAKER.clue: Implanted device that paces the heart; electrical stimulation over the chest and diathermy are contraindicated
PACEMAKER.rationale: The ipsilateral shoulder is often limited for several weeks so leads do not dislodge. Rate-responsive units may not raise heart rate the way a normal sinus node does.

ICD.clue: Implanted device that treats dangerous ventricular rhythms; keep exercise heart rate below its detection cutoff
ICD.rationale: Electrical stimulation over the chest and diathermy are contraindicated. A shock during exercise stops the session and prompts medical review.

DIGITALIS.clue: Drug that increases the force of the heartbeat; toxicity is more likely when potassium is low
DIGITALIS.rationale: Digoxin increases contractile force. Nausea, visual changes, and new arrhythmias suggest toxicity, which is more likely when potassium is low.

DIURETIC.clue: Drug that increases urine output and can waste potassium, causing cramps and arrhythmias
DIURETIC.rationale: It is used in heart failure and hypertension. Muscle cramps plus a low potassium are reported rather than treated as simple overuse.

STATIN.clue: Cholesterol drug that can cause muscle pain or, rarely, breakdown of muscle
STATIN.rationale: Unexplained soreness, weakness, or dark urine on this drug is reported. It is not assumed to be delayed-onset soreness from exercise.

STEROID.clue: Anti-inflammatory drug that with long use causes osteoporosis, proximal weakness, high blood sugar, and infection risk
STEROID.rationale: Doses are not stopped abruptly. Skin is fragile and blood pressure may be high, so aggressive stretching and unprotected impact are avoided.

INSULIN.clue: Hormone used in diabetes; exercise can lower blood sugar for many hours, and injection into the working muscle speeds absorption
INSULIN.rationale: Below about 70 mg/dL, carbohydrate is given and sugar is rechecked before exercise. Above about 250 to 300 mg/dL, especially with ketones, exercise is postponed.

GLUCOSE.clue: Blood sugar; exercise is generally avoided below about 70 mg/dL until carbohydrate is given
GLUCOSE.rationale: A value above about 250 mg/dL with ketones, or above about 300 mg/dL, is a reason to postpone exercise. Symptoms of a low value include sweating, shakiness, and confusion.

KETONES.clue: Acidic byproducts of fat metabolism; their presence with high blood sugar is a reason to postpone exercise
KETONES.rationale: They indicate insulin deficiency, especially in type 1 diabetes. Deep rapid breathing and fruity breath suggest ketoacidosis.

FRUITY.clue: Breath odor with high blood sugar, nausea, and deep rapid breathing that suggests ketoacidosis
FRUITY.rationale: Exercise is contraindicated. The patient needs urgent medical care, not insulin adjustment by the therapist.

HEMOGLOBIN.clue: Oxygen-carrying protein; many acute-care guidelines limit exercise to essential mobility below about 8 g/dL
HEMOGLOBIN.rationale: Between 8 and 10 g/dL, activity is often light and symptom-limited. The number is a guide, and dizziness or chest pain stops the session regardless.

HEMATOCRIT.clue: Percent of blood that is red cells; exercise is often limited below about 25 percent
HEMATOCRIT.rationale: It moves with hemoglobin. A symptomatic patient is not exercised just because the number is slightly above a cutoff.

PLATELET.clue: Cell fragment needed for clotting; counts below about 20,000 per microliter usually limit activity to essential mobility
PLATELET.rationale: Resistance and high fall-risk tasks are avoided because of bleeding. The oncology or medical team sets the limit for the facility.

INR.clue: Clotting measure used with warfarin; a higher value means slower clotting and more bleeding risk
INR.rationale: Therapeutic ranges are often about 2 to 3, higher for some mechanical valves. A markedly elevated value is a reason to avoid falls and deep soft-tissue work.

WARFARIN.clue: Oral anticoagulant monitored with INR; falls and deep soft-tissue work carry more bleeding risk when the value is high
WARFARIN.rationale: It does not dissolve an existing clot. Vitamin K intake is kept consistent, and the therapist does not adjust the dose.

HEPARIN.clue: Anticoagulant given by injection that limits extension of a clot; once it is effective, walking is usually allowed
HEPARIN.rationale: Massage and heat over a known deep-vein clot are contraindicated. Prolonged bed rest after anticoagulation has started is no longer the usual plan.

FEBRILE.clue: Having a fever; exercise is generally deferred above about 100 degrees Fahrenheit when systemic symptoms are present
FEBRILE.rationale: A fever can signal infection, including in a joint or a disc. The cause is identified rather than worked through.

DVT.clue: Clot in a deep vein; once anticoagulation has started, walking is generally safe, and massage or heat over the clot is not
DVT.rationale: Calf pain on dorsiflexion does not diagnose or exclude it. Unilateral swelling, warmth, and risk factors prompt duplex imaging.

VIRCHOW.clue: Triad of risk for thrombosis: stasis, vessel-wall injury, and hypercoagulability
VIRCHOW.rationale: Immobility, surgery, cancer, and estrogen therapy contribute. Prevention includes mobility and, when prescribed, anticoagulation or compression.

EMBOLUS.clue: A clot that has traveled, often from a leg vein to the lung; sudden dyspnea, chest pain, and falling saturation are an emergency
EMBOLUS.rationale: Exercise stops and emergency services are activated. A fat embolus after a long-bone fracture adds confusion and a petechial rash.

PETECHIAE.clue: Pinpoint hemorrhages that, with sudden confusion and dyspnea after a long-bone fracture, suggest fat embolism
PETECHIAE.rationale: The classic window is a day or two after the fracture. It is an emergency, not a skin irritation from a splint.

PAD.clue: Arterial disease that causes calf pain at a repeatable walking distance, relieved by standing rest
PAD.rationale: Supervised walking to moderate pain, then rest, and repeat, is first-line therapy. Pulses are diminished, and compression is avoided when the ankle-brachial index is low.

ABI.clue: Ratio of ankle systolic pressure to brachial systolic pressure; below 0.90 supports peripheral artery disease
ABI.rationale: Below about 0.40 disease is severe, and above about 1.40 vessels may be too calcified to compress. Standard compression is generally acceptable above about 0.80, reduced between 0.50 and 0.80, and avoided below about 0.50.

ARTERIAL.clue: Insufficiency: a cool pale limb, poor pulses, pain with elevation, and ulcers on toes or the lateral foot
ARTERIAL.rationale: Compression is avoided when the ankle-brachial index shows significant disease. Elevation that increases pain is the opposite of venous disease.

VENOUS.clue: Insufficiency: aching, hemosiderin staining, and edema that improve with elevation and compression when arteries are adequate
VENOUS.rationale: Ulcers are often near the medial malleolus, irregular, and moist. Compression is not applied until arterial supply is checked.

BUERGER.clue: Smoking-related vasculitis of small arteries that causes claudication and ischemic ulcers of the hands and feet
BUERGER.rationale: Stopping tobacco is the essential treatment. Elevation pallor and dependent redness are signs of arterial compromise that share this eponym.

RAYNAUD.clue: Episodic vasospasm of the digits with color change in the cold; cold modalities are contraindicated
RAYNAUD.rationale: Fingers turn white, then blue, then red as flow returns. Patients keep the hands warm and avoid ice packs.

NEUROGENIC.clue: Claudication from lumbar stenosis: leg pain with walking that eases with spinal flexion, unlike a fixed arterial distance
NEUROGENIC.rationale: A shopping cart that lets the patient flex often helps. Pulses are present, which separates it from arterial disease.

STENOSIS.clue: Narrowing of the spinal canal; lumbar symptoms increase with extension and ease with flexion
STENOSIS.rationale: Walking tolerance falls and sitting helps. Flexion-biased exercise is used when extension peripheralizes symptoms.

HNP.clue: Herniated nucleus pulposus; a posterolateral lumbar herniation typically compresses the traversing root, so L4–L5 affects L5
HNP.rationale: A far-lateral herniation instead compresses the exiting root. Central herniation can threaten bowel and bladder and is an emergency if saddle sensation or sphincter control changes.

DISC.clue: Intervertebral structure whose posterolateral herniation usually affects the traversing nerve root of the lower level
DISC.rationale: Repeated extension is used only when symptoms move out of the leg toward the spine. Flexion is preferred for stenosis and for many spondylolistheses.

REPEATED.clue: Spine movements selected because symptoms travel from the limb toward the spine rather than farther down the limb
REPEATED.rationale: The McKenzie approach uses this response to choose a direction. Extension is often tried for a posterior derangement and is stopped if pain moves farther into the limb.

HYPOMOBILE.clue: Lumbar finding in the prediction rule for patients likely to improve with manipulation, along with recent onset and no symptoms below the knee
HYPOMOBILE.rationale: The rule also uses hip internal rotation greater than about 35 degrees and a low work-related fear score. Meeting several items, not one, is what predicts response.

LYSIS.clue: Pars defect without slippage, often in adolescents who repeatedly extend the spine
LYSIS.rationale: Pain is worse with extension, and an oblique radiograph shows a collar on the scotty-dog outline. Flexion-biased activity is preferred.

LISTHESIS.clue: Forward slip of one vertebra on the one below, graded by how much of the body has slipped
LISTHESIS.rationale: Grade I is up to 25 percent, grade II to 50 percent, grade III to 75 percent, and grade IV beyond that. Extension is usually limited.

ANKYLOSING.clue: Spondylitis: inflammatory spinal fusion, often in young adults, with limited chest expansion and a flexed posture
ANKYLOSING.rationale: Stiffness lasts more than about an hour in the morning and improves with movement. Extension exercise and chest expansion are emphasized, and high-impact flexion is avoided.

BAMBOO.clue: Spine appearance of advanced ankylosing spondylitis, from bridges of bone between vertebrae
BAMBOO.rationale: The spine can fracture with minor trauma and the fracture is unstable. New pain after a fall in a fused spine is imaged, not mobilized.

SCOLIOSIS.clue: Lateral curvature with rotation, named by the convex side
SCOLIOSIS.rationale: In a growing child, moderate curves around 25 to 40 degrees are commonly braced, and curves approaching 45 to 50 degrees are often considered for surgery. A forward bend shows a rib hump on the convex side.

KYPHOSIS.clue: Excessive thoracic flexion curvature; a rigid adolescent form has vertebral wedging
KYPHOSIS.rationale: Scheuermann disease shows anterior wedging of several adjacent vertebrae. Extension exercise and, in a growing child with a larger curve, bracing are used.

SCHEUERMANN.clue: Disease: rigid juvenile kyphosis with anterior wedging of several vertebrae
SCHEUERMANN.rationale: It is structural, not a flexible postural curve. Extension-biased exercise is used, and bracing is considered while the patient is still growing.

LORDOSIS.clue: Excessive lumbar or cervical extension curvature; an anterior pelvic tilt increases the lumbar form
LORDOSIS.rationale: Hip-flexor and back-extensor tightness and weak abdominals are common contributors. It is a description of alignment, not a diagnosis by itself.

WHIPLASH.clue: Acceleration injury of the neck; prolonged collar use is avoided once serious injury is excluded, and early gentle movement is preferred
WHIPLASH.rationale: Neurologic deficit, midline tenderness, or a dangerous mechanism still requires imaging first. Soft collars do not stabilize an unstable spine.

RHEUMATOID.clue: Autoimmune synovitis that attacks joints symmetrically and can loosen the atlantoaxial joint
RHEUMATOID.rationale: Morning stiffness often lasts more than an hour. End-range cervical motion is avoided, and the hand may show ulnar drift, swan-neck, or boutonniere deformities.

STIFFNESS.clue: Morning tightness lasting more than about an hour suggests inflammatory arthritis, whereas a brief version is more typical of osteoarthritis
STIFFNESS.rationale: Inflammatory pain also improves with movement. Osteoarthritis tends to involve the distal finger joints, which rheumatoid disease usually spares.

HEBERDEN.clue: Nodes: bony enlargement of the distal finger joints in osteoarthritis
HEBERDEN.rationale: They are osteophytes, not rheumatoid nodules. The proximal finger joints can show Bouchard nodes in the same disease.

BOUCHARD.clue: Nodes: bony enlargement of the proximal finger joints in osteoarthritis
BOUCHARD.rationale: Rheumatoid arthritis prefers these joints and the knuckles but typically spares the distal joints. Nodes are bony and not hot synovitis.

DEVIATION.clue: Ulnar drift of the fingers at the knuckles, a common rheumatoid hand deformity
DEVIATION.rationale: The metacarpophalangeal joints sublux. Splints and joint-protection habits reduce deforming forces during daily tasks.

GOUT.clue: Crystal arthritis, often at the first metatarsophalangeal joint, with severe pain, redness, and swelling
GOUT.rationale: The acute joint is not mobilized vigorously. Recurrent disease can leave chalky deposits called tophi.

PODAGRA.clue: Gout of the first metatarsophalangeal joint
PODAGRA.rationale: The joint is hot, swollen, and too painful to walk on. It is distinguished from a neuropathic ulcer, which is usually painless.

TOPHUS.clue: Chalky deposit of urate crystals in chronic gout
TOPHUS.rationale: Common sites include the ear, olecranon, and toes. The deposit itself is not an acute hot joint, but the skin over it can break down.

SEPTIC.clue: Arthritis: one acutely hot joint with fever or inability to bear weight is infection until proven otherwise
SEPTIC.rationale: It is an emergency, including in a prosthetic joint. The joint is not exercised or injected by the therapist.

FROZEN.clue: Shoulder: progressive loss of active and passive motion, especially external rotation, from capsular contracture
FROZEN.rationale: The pattern follows the capsular order, with external rotation most limited. It is different from a cuff tear, which limits active motion more than passive.

CAPSULAR.clue: Pattern of range loss from an irritated joint capsule; at the shoulder, external rotation is limited more than abduction, which is limited more than internal rotation
CAPSULAR.rationale: At the hip the typical losses are flexion, abduction, and internal rotation. A loss that does not follow the pattern suggests a derangement or an extra-articular block.

CONGRUENT.clue: Close-packed position in which the capsule is taut and the surfaces fit best; mobilization is not performed there
CONGRUENT.rationale: Examples include full abduction and external rotation at the shoulder, extension with abduction and internal rotation at the hip, full extension at the knee, and full dorsiflexion at the ankle.

RESTING.clue: Open-packed position of greatest joint play, where mobilization is performed
RESTING.rationale: The shoulder rests near 55 degrees of abduction and 30 degrees of horizontal adduction. The hip rests near 30 degrees of flexion and abduction with slight external rotation, and the knee near 25 degrees of flexion.

CONCAVE.clue: Rule: when a hollow surface moves on a rounded one, the glide is in the same direction as the angular motion
CONCAVE.rationale: Open-chain knee flexion needs a posterior glide of the tibia, while a rounded humeral head glides inferiorly during abduction. The glide is parallel to the treatment plane.

MAITLAND.clue: Oscillatory mobilizations graded I to IV by amplitude and by where they sit in the range
MAITLAND.rationale: Grades I and II stay short of resistance and are used for pain, while grades III and IV reach resistance and are used for mobility. Grade V is a thrust.

KALTENBORN.clue: Sustained traction graded I to loosen, II to take up slack, and III to stretch
KALTENBORN.rationale: Glides are parallel to the treatment plane and distraction is perpendicular to it. Grade I neutralizes compression without stretching the capsule.

GLIDE.clue: Translatoric joint play parallel to the treatment plane, used to restore a specific range
GLIDE.rationale: Direction follows the convex-concave rule. It is a slide, not the roll that occurs with the bone's angular motion.

SPIN.clue: Rotation of one joint surface around a stationary axis, as at the radial head during pronation and supination
SPIN.rationale: Most joint motions combine roll and glide, with this rotation as a third component. Mobilization techniques usually restore the glide.

BONY.clue: Hard end-feel from bone contacting bone, normal at elbow extension
BONY.rationale: A hard stop where the end-feel should be soft or firm is abnormal. Elbow flexion, by contrast, normally stops in soft tissue.

FIRM.clue: Normal end-feel from capsule or ligament stretch, as at shoulder external rotation
FIRM.rationale: It is abnormal when it appears where a hard stop is expected, or earlier in the range than the other side. A springy rebound is a different, abnormal feel.

SOFT.clue: Normal end-feel from tissue compression, as when the calf meets the thigh at the end of knee flexion
SOFT.rationale: A soft, boggy stop from swelling is abnormal. A springy block suggests a meniscus or loose body.

SPRINGY.clue: Rebounding end-feel that suggests a meniscal block or a loose body
SPRINGY.rationale: The knee does not reach a firm or bony stop. It is abnormal in every joint.

BOGGY.clue: Soft, mushy end-feel of joint effusion or acute inflammation
BOGGY.rationale: It replaces the normal stop. A hot boggy joint with fever is treated as possible infection.

SPASM.clue: End-feel in which muscle guarding stops the motion before the anatomic limit
SPASM.rationale: It is abnormal and protective. Forcing past it can increase injury.

CREEP.clue: Gradual lengthening of connective tissue under a constant low load, the basis of prolonged stretching
CREEP.rationale: Stress relaxation is the related fall in tension when length is held. Both justify low-load, long-duration stretching for contracture.

SPINDLE.clue: Muscle receptor that senses stretch and triggers the stretch reflex
SPINDLE.rationale: A quick stretch facilitates the muscle through this receptor. A slow prolonged stretch is used when the goal is length, not a reflex contraction.

GOLGI.clue: Tendon organ that senses tension and can inhibit the muscle being stretched
GOLGI.rationale: Contract-relax stretching uses this autogenic inhibition. The contraction is followed by a deeper stretch of the same muscle.

AUTOOGENIC.clue: Inhibition of a muscle after it contracts, mediated by the Golgi tendon organ and used in contract-relax stretching
AUTOOGENIC.rationale: The tight muscle contracts, then relaxes, and the stretch is taken further. Reciprocal inhibition instead uses contraction of the opposing muscle.

RECIPROCAL.clue: Inhibition of a muscle when its antagonist contracts, which can be used to stretch the inhibited muscle
RECIPROCAL.rationale: Contraction of the quadriceps can help the hamstrings lengthen. It is a different mechanism from inhibition of the muscle that just contracted.

ISOMETRIC.clue: Contraction that produces force without visible joint motion
ISOMETRIC.rationale: It is useful when motion is painful or forbidden, but strength gains are fairly specific to the angle trained. Breath-holding during the hold is avoided.

ISOTONIC.clue: Contraction against a constant external load in which the muscle shortens or lengthens and the joint moves
ISOTONIC.rationale: Free weights approximate this condition. Concentric work shortens the muscle and eccentric work lengthens it.

ISOKINETIC.clue: Contraction at a preset angular speed on a dynamometer, with resistance matching the force the patient produces
ISOKINETIC.rationale: The speed stays constant through the range. It is used for testing and for training when a dynamometer is available.

CONCENTRIC.clue: Shortening contraction in which internal torque exceeds the external load
CONCENTRIC.rationale: It accelerates the limb. It produces less force and less delayed soreness than a lengthening contraction of the same muscle.

ECCENTRIC.clue: Lengthening contraction in which the external load exceeds internal torque; it is linked to delayed-onset muscle soreness
ECCENTRIC.rationale: It produces high force and is used in later tendon rehabilitation. It is avoided in the early care of muscular dystrophy and of an irritable nerve injury such as Guillain-Barré.

PLYOMETRIC.clue: Exercise that uses a rapid lengthening contraction followed immediately by shortening, the stretch-shortening cycle
PLYOMETRIC.rationale: A strength base and 48 hours of recovery between sessions are usual precautions. It is not introduced into an acute or unstable joint.

OPEN.clue: Kinetic chain in which the distal segment is free, as in a seated knee extension
OPEN.rationale: Motion is usually non-weight-bearing and more isolated. After anterior cruciate reconstruction, resisted extension in this chain near full extension is limited early.

CLOSED.clue: Kinetic chain in which the distal segment is fixed, as in a squat
CLOSED.rationale: Several joints move together under body weight. Early anterior cruciate rehabilitation often allows a limited squat range before loaded open-chain extension near full extension.

SAID.clue: Principle that the body adapts specifically to the demands imposed, so training should match the task
SAID.rationale: Strength work does not automatically become endurance, and a straight-plane exercise may not transfer to a diagonal sport skill. The task is practiced, not only its pieces.

OVERLOAD.clue: Training principle that a tissue must be stressed beyond its usual load to adapt
OVERLOAD.rationale: The increase is progressive rather than sudden. Too large a jump is a common cause of overuse injury.

PROGRESSION.clue: Training principle of gradually increasing load, volume, or complexity so tissue can adapt
PROGRESSION.rationale: One variable changes at a time. Pain that lasts or worsens the next day is a sign to reduce the dose.

DETRAINING.clue: Loss of training adaptations after activity is reduced; aerobic gains fade within weeks
DETRAINING.rationale: Illness and immobilization reverse strength and endurance. Restarting at the previous load is a common cause of injury.

DOMS.clue: Muscle pain that peaks a day or two after unaccustomed eccentric exercise and is not an acute injury
DOMS.rationale: Lactate has already cleared and is not the cause. It is different from pain during the exercise or from rhabdomyolysis with dark urine.

PHOSPHAGEN.clue: Immediate energy system using stored phosphocreatine for maximal efforts lasting only several seconds
PHOSPHAGEN.rationale: Glycolysis then supports intense work up to about two minutes. Longer efforts depend mainly on aerobic metabolism.

GLYCOLYSIS.clue: Breakdown of glucose that supplies energy for intense efforts lasting up to about two minutes and produces lactate
GLYCOLYSIS.rationale: Lactate is cleared within about an hour and does not cause next-day soreness. The aerobic system dominates efforts that last many minutes.

LACTATE.clue: Byproduct that rises when glycolysis outpaces aerobic metabolism; it is not the cause of next-day muscle soreness
LACTATE.rationale: The threshold is the intensity where blood levels begin to climb. Soreness a day later is related to eccentric muscle damage.

SLOW.clue: Twitch fiber, type I: fatigue-resistant and oxidative, abundant in postural muscle such as soleus
SLOW.rationale: Type II fibers are larger and fatigue faster and are used for power. Training can shift metabolic properties but does not turn one anatomic fiber into the other overnight.

FAST.clue: Twitch fiber, type II: larger and more fatigable, recruited for powerful movements
FAST.rationale: Type IIx is the most glycolytic. A muscle such as gastrocnemius has more of these fibers than soleus, which is predominantly slow.

AGONIST.clue: Muscle that produces the desired motion, also called the prime mover
AGONIST.rationale: The opposing muscle is the antagonist. A stabilizer holds an adjacent segment so the prime mover can act.

ANTAGONIST.clue: Muscle that opposes the prime mover and can be inhibited when the prime mover contracts
ANTAGONIST.rationale: Reciprocal inhibition uses this relationship during stretching. Co-contraction of both muscles stabilizes a joint.

MMT.clue: Ordinal strength grades from 0, no contraction, to 5, which holds against gravity and maximal resistance
MMT.rationale: Grade 3 moves through the full range against gravity with no added resistance. Grade 2 moves through the full range only with gravity eliminated.

TRACE.clue: Manual muscle grade with a palpable contraction but no joint motion
TRACE.rationale: It is grade 1. Grade 2, poor, completes the range with gravity eliminated.

POOR.clue: Manual muscle grade 2: full range with gravity eliminated, but not against gravity
POOR.rationale: A grade of 3, fair, completes the range against gravity without added resistance. Plus and minus grades describe partial range within a level.

FAIR.clue: Manual muscle grade 3: full range against gravity with no added resistance
FAIR.rationale: Grade 4 holds against moderate resistance and grade 5 against maximal resistance. Grade 3 is the first grade that can lift the limb against gravity.

GOOD.clue: Manual muscle grade 4: full range against gravity and moderate resistance, but the hold yields somewhat
GOOD.rationale: Grade 5 does not yield to maximal resistance. These grades are ordinal, so the gap from 4 to 5 is not a measured unit of force.

NORMAL.clue: Manual muscle grade 5: full range against gravity and maximal resistance
NORMAL.rationale: It is the top ordinal grade, not a measurement in newtons. A dynamometer is used when a number of force units is needed.

BREAK.clue: Strength test in which the examiner tries to overcome a contraction the patient is holding
BREAK.rationale: The make test instead has the patient build force against a fixed resistance. Break tests often record higher values.

MAKE.clue: Strength test in which the patient builds force against a resistance that does not move
MAKE.rationale: A handheld dynamometer is often used. It differs from a test in which the examiner overpowers a held contraction.

ROM.clue: Arc of motion at a joint, measured in degrees with a goniometer aligned to bony landmarks
ROM.rationale: Active motion is produced by the patient, passive motion by the examiner, and active-assisted motion by both. A capsular pattern is a characteristic loss of this arc.

AROM.clue: Range produced by the patient's own muscles, without help from the examiner
AROM.rationale: It requires strength of at least fair for a full arc against gravity. Pain during it but not during passive motion suggests a contractile tissue.

PROM.clue: Range produced entirely by the examiner, used when the patient cannot or should not activate the muscle
PROM.rationale: It maintains mobility and shows the anatomic limit. A hard, empty, or springy stop is interpreted as an end-feel.

AAROM.clue: Range in which the patient starts the motion and receives help to finish it
AAROM.rationale: It is used when strength is below fair or when active motion must be assisted after surgery. It sits between passive and fully active motion.

GONIOMETER.clue: Instrument aligned with bony landmarks to measure joint range in degrees
GONIOMETER.rationale: The axis is placed over the joint axis and the arms along the moving and stationary segments. The same landmarks are used each time so change is real.

DYNAMOMETER.clue: Device that quantifies grip or muscle force; grip is usually tested with the handle in the second position
DYNAMOMETER.rationale: The mean of trials is recorded, and the arm position is standardized. A change smaller than measurement error may not be real improvement.

GAIT.clue: Manner of walking; a cycle is the time from one heel contact to the next contact of the same foot
GAIT.rationale: Stance is about 60 percent and swing about 40 percent. Two periods of double support total about 20 percent and disappear in running.

CADENCE.clue: Step rate, normally about 110 to 120 steps per minute in adults
CADENCE.rationale: Speed equals this rate times step length. A short step with a high rate is typical of Parkinson disease.

STRIDE.clue: Distance or time from one heel contact to the next contact of the same foot, normally about 1.4 meters
STRIDE.rationale: It contains two steps. A reduced value with a wide base suggests impaired balance or a short, painful stance.

STEP.clue: Distance from one heel contact to the next contact of the opposite foot
STEP.rationale: Two successive ones make a stride. The painful limb often shows a shorter stance time, which shortens the opposite step.

STANCE.clue: Portion of the gait cycle when the foot is on the ground, about 60 percent
STANCE.rationale: It includes initial contact, loading response, midstance, terminal stance, and preswing. Single-limb support equals the opposite swing.

SWING.clue: Portion of the gait cycle when the foot is off the ground, about 40 percent
SWING.rationale: It includes initial swing, midswing, and terminal swing. Foot clearance depends on hip flexion, knee flexion, and ankle dorsiflexion.

DOUBLE.clue: Support period when both feet are on the ground, about 10 percent at each end of stance and absent in running
DOUBLE.rationale: It lengthens when walking slows or balance is poor. Running replaces it with a flight phase.

SINGLE.clue: Limb support during gait, about 40 percent of the cycle, equal to the opposite swing
SINGLE.rationale: The hip abductors keep the pelvis level during it. Weakness produces a drop of the opposite side of the pelvis.

INITIAL.clue: Contact: the instant the foot touches, starting the gait cycle, with the ankle near neutral
INITIAL.rationale: Loading response follows, as the foot lowers to the floor under eccentric control of the anterior tibialis. The knee flexes slightly to absorb shock.

LOADING.clue: Response: the first about 10 percent of the gait cycle, when the foot flattens and shock is absorbed
LOADING.rationale: Tibialis anterior works eccentrically to prevent foot slap, and the quadriceps work eccentrically to control knee flexion. It is a double-support interval.

MIDSTANCE.clue: Single-limb interval from opposite toe-off until the body is over the stance foot
MIDSTANCE.rationale: The plantarflexors control forward advancement of the tibia. The hip abductors prevent the opposite pelvis from dropping.

TERMINAL.clue: Stance from heel rise until the opposite foot contacts, with the body ahead of the stance foot
TERMINAL.rationale: The plantarflexors peak to control dorsiflexion and the hip extends. Preswing, the second double-support interval, follows.

PRESWING.clue: Final about 10 percent of stance, from opposite initial contact to toe-off
PRESWING.rationale: The knee flexes and the ankle plantarflexes as weight shifts to the other limb. It is the second double-support period.

MIDSWING.clue: Interval when the swinging limb passes the stance limb and the tibia is roughly vertical
MIDSWING.rationale: Tibialis anterior holds the ankle so the toes clear. Hip flexors have already advanced the thigh, and the hamstrings begin to decelerate it.

VELOCITY.clue: Walking speed; about 0.8 m/s is often used as a threshold for community walking, and faster speeds are needed to cross streets
VELOCITY.rationale: It is the product of cadence and step length. A 10-meter walk at usual and fast pace is the common clinical measure.

FLIGHT.clue: Phase present in running and absent in walking, when neither foot is on the ground
FLIGHT.rationale: Walking always has double support. Running has this airborne interval and higher forces at the joints.

ANTALGIC.clue: Gait that shortens stance time on a painful limb
ANTALGIC.rationale: The opposite step becomes shorter. It is a pain strategy, not a neurologic pattern, and the cause of pain is treated.

STEPPAGE.clue: High stepping gait that clears a foot that cannot dorsiflex
STEPPAGE.rationale: It follows common fibular palsy or an L4 root lesion. The foot may also slap at contact if the dorsiflexors cannot lower it slowly.

VAULTING.clue: Clearance strategy that plantarflexes the stance limb so a long or stiff swing limb can pass
VAULTING.rationale: A prosthesis that is too long, a locked knee, or a foot in too much plantarflexion produces it. Hip hiking and circumduction are other clearance strategies.

HIKE.clue: Pelvic elevation in swing used to clear a long limb or a foot that does not dorsiflex
HIKE.rationale: Quadratus lumborum lifts the pelvis. It is a compensation, and the cause of poor clearance is addressed.

FESTINATING.clue: Parkinson gait of short, accelerating steps with the trunk leaning forward
FESTINATING.rationale: Turning is en bloc and arm swing is reduced. Visual or auditory cues can enlarge the steps.

SHUFFLING.clue: Parkinson gait pattern with short steps and reduced foot clearance
SHUFFLING.rationale: Festination and freezing in doorways may accompany it. Cues and large-amplitude practice are used during the medication on-period.

SCISSOR.clue: Gait of excessive hip adduction so the swing limb crosses midline, typical of spastic diplegia
SCISSOR.rationale: Adductor tone and weakness of the abductors contribute. An equinus or crouch pattern may be present at the same time.

CROUCH.clue: Gait of excessive hip and knee flexion, often with excessive ankle dorsiflexion, seen in cerebral palsy
CROUCH.rationale: Weak plantarflexors or an overlengthened heel cord cannot control the tibia. It is different from toe-walking equinus.

WIDE.clue: Base of gait seen with sensory loss or cerebellar dysfunction, the feet placed apart for stability
WIDE.rationale: Normal walking uses only a few centimeters of base. A positive Romberg test suggests the sensory form.

ANKLE.clue: Balance strategy for small disturbances on a firm surface, using distal-to-proximal muscles
ANKLE.rationale: A forward sway recruits gastrocnemius, then hamstrings, then paraspinals. A backward sway recruits tibialis anterior, then quadriceps, then abdominals.

SWAY.clue: Hip balance response for a larger disturbance or a narrow surface: abdominals and quadriceps correct a forward body lean, and paraspinals and hamstrings correct a backward one
SWAY.rationale: Activation is proximal to distal, the opposite order of the ankle strategy. A still larger disturbance requires a step.

STRATEGY.clue: Stepping response that creates a new base when an ankle or hip response cannot keep the center of mass over the feet
STRATEGY.rationale: It is used for large or fast disturbances. People who will not take a step have a higher fall risk.

CTSIB.clue: Balance test that varies vision and the surface to see which senses the patient relies on
CTSIB.rationale: Trouble only when the eyes are closed suggests visual dependence. Trouble on foam with the eyes closed suggests the vestibular system cannot be used when vision and surface input are both unavailable.

BOS.clue: Area under and between the feet; balance is lost when the center of mass moves outside it and no step is taken
BOS.rationale: A cane enlarges it. A narrower base, as in tandem stance, makes the same sway harder to control.

BERG.clue: 14-item balance scale scored to 56; scores at or below 45 are a commonly used fall-risk cutoff in older adults
BERG.rationale: Items include sit-to-stand, turning, and single-leg stance. It has a ceiling effect for active community ambulators.

TINETTI.clue: Performance test of balance and gait scored to 28; scores below 19 are often classed as high fall risk
TINETTI.rationale: Balance items and gait items are added. Lower scores mean higher risk, and the test includes an armless-chair rise.

TUG.clue: Timed test of rising, walking 3 meters, turning, and sitting back down
TUG.rationale: Times beyond about 13.5 seconds have been linked to higher fall risk in community-dwelling older adults. The chair has arms and the patient uses the usual device.

DGI.clue: Eight-item walking test that includes head turns and obstacles, scored to 24
DGI.rationale: Scores of 19 or below are associated with fall risk in older adults. The functional gait assessment adds items and is used when this test is too easy.

FGA.clue: Ten-item walking test scored to 30 that adds tasks to the dynamic gait index
FGA.rationale: A score of 22 or below suggests increased fall risk. It is less limited by a ceiling than the shorter gait index.

REACH.clue: Forward test of how far a standing person can extend the fist; less than about 6 inches is associated with high fall risk
REACH.rationale: The feet stay planted. A value between about 6 and 10 inches is often described as a moderate risk.

CHAIR.clue: Stand test that counts how many times an older adult can rise in 30 seconds, screening leg strength and fall risk
CHAIR.rationale: Arms are crossed, and fewer repetitions than the age norm indicates weakness. A five-times version is timed instead of counted.

WALK.clue: Six-minute test of distance covered at a self-selected pace, with rests allowed
WALK.rationale: It reflects functional endurance. The patient is not coached to speed up, and oxygen saturation is watched in pulmonary disease.

FIM.clue: 18-item disability scale scored from 1, total assist, to 7, independent, with a total from 18 to 126
FIM.rationale: Thirteen items are motor and five are cognitive. Lower scores mean more assistance and a higher burden of care.

BARTHEL.clue: Index of basic daily activities scored to 100; lower scores mean greater dependence
BARTHEL.rationale: It covers feeding, bathing, dressing, toileting, transfers, and mobility. It is less detailed than the 18-item rehabilitation scale.

LAWTON.clue: Scale of instrumental activities such as telephone use, shopping, cooking, medicines, and finances
LAWTON.rationale: These tasks are more complex than basic self-care. Impairment here can appear before loss of bathing or dressing.

ADL.clue: Basic self-care tasks such as bathing, dressing, toileting, transferring, continence, and feeding
ADL.rationale: Instrumental tasks such as shopping and managing money are a separate, higher set. Therapy goals name the specific task, not only this abbreviation.

OSWESTRY.clue: Low-back disability questionnaire reported as a percentage; higher scores mean greater disability
OSWESTRY.rationale: Ten sections include pain, walking, and sitting. It is condition-specific, unlike a generic health survey.

NDI.clue: Neck disability index: ten items, often reported as a percentage, with higher scores meaning greater disability
NDI.rationale: It parallels the low-back questionnaire. Headache, reading, and driving are among the items.

LEFS.clue: Lower-extremity functional scale of 20 items scored to 80; higher scores mean better function
LEFS.rationale: A change of about 9 points is often considered meaningful. It is the opposite direction of a disability index, where higher is worse.

DASH.clue: Questionnaire of arm, shoulder, and hand disability scored from 0 to 100; higher scores mean more disability
DASH.rationale: A shorter 11-item form is scored the same way. Work and sport modules can be added.

WOMAC.clue: Osteoarthritis index for the hip or knee covering pain, stiffness, and function; higher scores mean worse symptoms
WOMAC.rationale: It is not scored like the knee injury outcome score, on which 100 means no symptoms. Direction of the scale must be checked before interpreting change.

KOOS.clue: Knee injury and osteoarthritis outcome score on which 100 means no symptoms and 0 means extreme problems
KOOS.rationale: Subscales include pain, symptoms, daily activities, sport, and quality of life. A rising score is improvement.

HOOS.clue: Hip disability and osteoarthritis outcome score on which 100 means no disability
HOOS.rationale: It is the hip counterpart of the knee outcome score. Higher is better, unlike the WOMAC index.

PSFS.clue: Scale on which the patient rates up to five personal activities from 0 to 10; higher means better function
PSFS.rationale: A change of about 2 points on the average is often considered meaningful. The activities are chosen by the patient.

NPRS.clue: Pain scale from 0 to 10; a change of about 2 points is often considered meaningful
NPRS.rationale: It is a number the patient picks, unlike a mark on a 10-centimeter line. The same anchors are used at each visit.

VAS.clue: Pain scale on which the patient marks intensity on a 10-centimeter line
VAS.rationale: The distance in millimeters is the score. It is harder to use by telephone than a 0-to-10 number.

MCID.clue: Smallest change in a score that a patient would identify as important
MCID.rationale: It is not the same as the smallest change that exceeds measurement error. A measure is most useful when important change is larger than error.

MDC.clue: Smallest change that exceeds measurement error; a smaller change may be noise
MDC.rationale: It is a statistical property of the test. A change can exceed it and still be too small for the patient to value.

GLASGOW.clue: Coma scale of eye, verbal, and motor responses from 3 to 15; 8 or below indicates severe impairment of consciousness
GLASGOW.rationale: Eyes are scored to 4, verbal to 5, and motor to 6. Motor scores of 3 and 2 correspond to abnormal flexion and extension posturing.

RANCHOS.clue: Levels of cognitive function after brain injury, from no response at level I through purposeful behavior at the higher levels
RANCHOS.rationale: Level IV is confused and agitated, and the revised scale extends to level X. Agitated patients need a calm setting rather than repeated orientation quizzes.

NIHSS.clue: Stroke severity scale; higher scores mean a larger neurologic deficit
NIHSS.rationale: It is used in acute care and includes language, visual fields, and limb strength. It does not replace functional measures such as gait speed.

FUGLMEYER.clue: Stroke motor scale of reflex, synergy, and isolated movement; higher scores mean better recovery
FUGLMEYER.rationale: It follows the typical progression out of obligatory patterns. It is an impairment scale, not a measure of whether the patient can walk at home.

RIVERMEAD.clue: Mobility index after stroke that scores items from bed mobility through running; higher scores mean better mobility
RIVERMEAD.rationale: The maximum is 15. It is quick and does not require equipment, but it is coarse for patients who already walk in the community.

CVA.clue: Cerebrovascular accident: an ischemic or hemorrhagic stroke causing sudden focal neurologic deficits
CVA.rationale: Face and arm weakness greater than the leg suggests the middle cerebral artery. Leg-predominant weakness suggests the anterior cerebral artery.

MCA.clue: Artery whose stroke weakens the contralateral face and arm more than the leg and can cause aphasia or neglect
MCA.rationale: A dominant-hemisphere lesion, usually left, affects language. A nondominant lesion, usually right, causes neglect and spatial problems.

ACA.clue: Artery whose stroke weakens the contralateral leg more than the arm and can change frontal behavior
ACA.rationale: Urinary incontinence and abulia can occur. Arm strength may be relatively spared, unlike a middle-cerebral lesion.

PCA.clue: Artery whose stroke can cause contralateral visual-field loss and, if the thalamus is involved, sensory change
PCA.rationale: Macular vision is sometimes spared because of collateral supply to the occipital pole. Memory can be affected if the medial temporal lobe is involved.

BASILAR.clue: Artery formed by the vertebral arteries; occlusion can cause brainstem signs and locked-in syndrome
BASILAR.rationale: Locked-in syndrome spares consciousness and often vertical eye movement while the limbs and speech are paralyzed. It is not a vegetative state.

LOCKED.clue: In syndrome: quadriplegia and loss of speech with preserved consciousness and vertical eye movement, classically from a ventral pontine lesion
LOCKED.rationale: Communication uses blinking or vertical gaze. The person is awake, which separates this state from coma.

WATERSHED.clue: Infarct at the border of two arterial territories, often from low perfusion, that can weaken the proximal limbs
WATERSHED.rationale: The man-in-the-barrel pattern spares the hands and face relative to the shoulders. It follows hypotension more often than an embolus to one branch.

LACUNAR.clue: Small deep infarct from a penetrating artery, often pure motor or pure sensory, without aphasia or neglect
LACUNAR.rationale: The internal capsule and thalamus are typical sites. Cortical signs such as aphasia point away from this type.

CAPSULE.clue: Internal structure carrying corticospinal fibers; a small lacune there can cause a dense hemiparesis
CAPSULE.rationale: The posterior limb carries motor fibers to the opposite body. Sensory fibers run nearby in the thalamus, not in this motor bundle.

HOMUNCULUS.clue: Map of the body on the motor and sensory cortices, with the face and hand occupying large areas
HOMUNCULUS.rationale: The leg is on the medial surface, in anterior-cerebral territory. The face and arm are on the lateral surface, in middle-cerebral territory.

NEGLECT.clue: Inattention to one side, usually the left after a right parietal lesion
NEGLECT.rationale: The patient may ignore food, the left limbs, or obstacles. Scanning cues and a safe environment are used, and insight is often poor.

APHASIA.clue: Language impairment after a dominant, usually left, hemisphere lesion
APHASIA.rationale: Broca aphasia is nonfluent with relatively spared comprehension, and Wernicke aphasia is fluent with poor comprehension. Dysarthria, by contrast, is a motor speech problem with language intact.

BROCA.clue: Nonfluent aphasia from a frontal lesion: speech is effortful and comprehension is relatively preserved
BROCA.rationale: The patient is often frustrated and aware. Yes-no questions and time to respond are more useful than rapid open-ended questions.

WERNICKE.clue: Fluent aphasia from a temporal lesion: speech is effortless but empty, and comprehension is poor
WERNICKE.rationale: The patient may be unaware of the errors. Gestures and demonstration help more than long verbal explanations.

ARCUATE.clue: Fasciculus connecting comprehension and speech areas; a lesion causes fluent speech with poor repetition and relatively spared comprehension
ARCUATE.rationale: This is conduction aphasia. Naming may also suffer, but the striking deficit is repetition.

DYSARTHRIA.clue: Motor speech disorder from weakness or incoordination of the speech muscles; language itself is intact
