BILATERAL.rationale: Both head-impulse tests are abnormal. The patient cannot rely on adaptation the way a one-sided loss can.

UNILATERAL.clue: Vestibular loss that produces an abnormal head impulse toward the weak side and can improve with gaze-stability and habituation exercises
UNILATERAL.rationale: Acute nystagmus beats away from the lesion and is reduced by looking at a target. Falls tend toward the weak side.

BRANDT.clue: Daroff exercises: repeated side-lying movements used as habituation for positional vertigo when a single repositioning maneuver is not the plan
BRANDT.rationale: Symptoms are expected and should decrease over days. They are not a substitute for ruling out a central cause.

MENIERE.clue: Inner-ear disorder with episodic vertigo, fluctuating hearing loss, tinnitus, and aural fullness
MENIERE.rationale: Attacks last longer than the seconds of positional debris. Therapy does not replace medical management of the acute spells.

ACOUSTIC.clue: Neuroma of cranial nerve VIII that can cause one-sided hearing loss, tinnitus, and imbalance
ACOUSTIC.rationale: A large tumor can also affect the facial or trigeminal nerve. Gradual one-sided hearing loss is referred, not treated as simple wax.

TMJ.clue: Joint whose opening combines rotation and then translation; the chin deviates toward a hypomobile side
TMJ.rationale: Normal opening is about 40 millimeters, or about three fingers. A click suggests a disc that reduces, and a closed lock suggests one that does not.

PTERYGOID.clue: Lateral muscle that helps open and protrude the jaw; acting alone it deviates the chin to the opposite side
PTERYGOID.rationale: The medial muscle helps close the jaw, along with the masseter and temporalis. All are innervated by the mandibular division of cranial nerve V.

MORO.clue: Infant reflex: a sudden head drop abducts then adducts the arms; it is normally integrated by about 6 months
MORO.rationale: Persistence interferes with head control and sitting. An asymmetric response can indicate a brachial plexus or clavicle injury.

ATNR.clue: Fencing reflex: turning the head extends the face-side limbs and flexes the skull-side limbs; it integrates by about 4 to 6 months
ATNR.rationale: Persistence blocks rolling and bringing the hand to the mouth. It should not dominate movement once the infant is reaching in midline.

STNR.clue: Reflex in which neck flexion flexes the arms and extends the legs, and neck extension does the opposite
STNR.rationale: It appears around 4 to 6 months and should integrate by about 8 to 12 months so hands-and-knees crawling can emerge.

TLR.clue: Reflex driven by head position: prone increases flexion tone and supine increases extension tone
TLR.rationale: It is normally integrated by about 6 months. Persistence blocks anti-gravity control and rolling.

GALANT.clue: Infant reflex: stroking beside the spine curves the trunk toward that side; it integrates by about 2 months
GALANT.rationale: Persistence can contribute to scoliosis or delay symmetrical trunk control. It is present at birth.

PALMAR.clue: Grasp reflex: pressure in the infant palm flexes the fingers; it integrates by about 4 to 6 months
PALMAR.rationale: The plantar version persists longer, often until 9 to 12 months. Voluntary grasp replaces the palmar form.

ROOTING.clue: Infant reflex: a stroke on the cheek turns the head toward the stimulus; it integrates by about 3 months
ROOTING.rationale: It supports early feeding. Persistence past that age can interfere with voluntary head control.

PARACHUTE.clue: Forward protective extension of the arms when an infant is tipped; it appears around 6 to 9 months and persists for life
PARACHUTE.rationale: Sideways protection appears a little later and backward protection later still. These reactions do not integrate.

LANDAU.clue: Reflex in which an infant held horizontally extends the head, trunk, and hips, like a brief superman posture
LANDAU.rationale: It appears around 3 to 4 months and integrates by about 12 to 24 months. Poor extension in this position suggests low tone.

STEPPING.clue: Primitive reflex: an infant held upright with the feet touching makes alternating steps; it integrates by about 2 months
STEPPING.rationale: It is not mature walking. Voluntary walking appears near the end of the first year.

RIGHTING.clue: Reactions that orient the head and trunk and underlie rolling in the first months
RIGHTING.rationale: Neck and body forms appear before equilibrium reactions. They persist in modified form as postural control matures.

PROTECTIVE.clue: Extension reactions of the arms that appear from about 6 months and persist to prevent a fall
PROTECTIVE.rationale: Forward appears first, then sideways, then backward. Absence in an older infant is a motor red flag.

CREEPING.clue: Hands-and-knees locomotion that typically appears around 8 to 10 months
CREEPING.rationale: Belly crawling often precedes it. Not every child uses this pattern, but absence of any floor mobility by the end of the first year is followed closely.

CRUISING.clue: Walking sideways while holding furniture, typically around 10 to 12 months
CRUISING.rationale: Independent walking often follows within a few months. A wide base and short steps are expected at first.

PINCER.clue: Grasp of a small object between the thumb and index finger, typically emerging by about 12 months
PINCER.rationale: An inferior form appears a little earlier. Persistent palmar raking without a thumb-finger grasp is a fine-motor concern.

ROLLING.clue: Segmental rotation from supine to prone that typically appears around 5 to 6 months
ROLLING.rationale: Prone to supine often comes first, around 4 to 5 months. A persistent log roll suggests the infant is not yet dissociating the trunk.

SUPPORT.clue: Primitive reflex: contact of the balls of the feet causes rigid leg extension and integrates by about 2 months
SUPPORT.rationale: Persistence interferes with standing balance and walking. It is different from later protective and equilibrium reactions.

BALANCE.clue: Reactions that restore the center of mass when it is pushed outside the base; they appear in sitting before standing and persist
BALANCE.rationale: Sitting reactions emerge around 7 to 8 months and standing reactions through the second year. They are tested by tipping the support surface.

SENSITIVITY.clue: Proportion of people with a condition who test positive; a sensitive test that is negative helps rule the condition out
SENSITIVITY.rationale: The mnemonic is SnNOut. A screening test is built to be sensitive so cases are not missed.

SPECIFICITY.clue: Proportion of people without a condition who test negative; a specific test that is positive helps rule the condition in
SPECIFICITY.rationale: The mnemonic is SpPIn. A confirmatory test is built to be specific so false positives are few.

SNOUT.clue: Mnemonic that a sensitive test, when negative, helps rule a diagnosis out
SNOUT.rationale: It is the companion of the mnemonic for a specific test that is positive. Neither replaces the clinical picture.

SPPIN.clue: Mnemonic that a specific test, when positive, helps rule a diagnosis in
SPPIN.rationale: A positive result on a low-specificity test still leaves many false positives. Prevalence changes how often a positive result is true.

RELIABILITY.clue: Consistency of a measure; intra-rater is the same tester over time, and inter-rater is agreement between testers
RELIABILITY.rationale: A measure can be consistent and still invalid if it measures the wrong thing. Both properties are reported for outcome tools.

VALIDITY.clue: Degree to which a test measures what it claims to measure
VALIDITY.rationale: Content, criterion, and construct forms ask different questions. Reliability is necessary but not sufficient for it.
